topics.t: Relations recap: empty and universal relations
topics.h: Your school timetable quietly pairs every student with a section. That pairing is a relation, and Class XII starts by asking what kind of relation it is.
p: A relation R from set A to set B is any subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R we write a R b. A relation on A is a subset of A × A.
If n(A) = m and n(B) = n, then A × B has mn ordered pairs, so there are 2^(mn) relations from A to B.
A function f: A → B is a relation in which every element of A has exactly one image in B. A is the domain, B the codomain, and the set of images is the range (range ⊆ codomain).
Empty relation: no element of A is related to any element, R = φ ⊆ A × A.
Universal relation: every element is related to every element, R = A × A. Empty and universal relations are called trivial relations.

ex.q: A = {students of a school}. R = {(a, b): a and b study in the same school}. S = {(a, b): the difference of the heights of a and b is more than 3 km}. Classify R and S.
st: Any two students of this school are in the same school, so every pair (a, b) is in R.
So R = A × A, the universal relation.
No two students can differ in height by 3 km, so no pair is in S.
So S = φ, the empty relation.
ex.a: R is universal; S is empty.

topics.rl: When IRCTC links each PNR number to exactly one passenger list, it is using a function. When it links stations to all trains that halt there, it is a relation that need not be a function.

rv.summary: A relation from A to B is any subset of A × B; the empty relation has no pairs and the universal relation is all of A × A. A function is a relation giving each element of A exactly one image.
focus: Count relations: 2^(mn) when n(A) = m, n(B) = n
Identify empty and universal relations from a rule
Tell a function from a relation; find the range of a function
remember: Relation on A: any subset of A × A
Number of relations from A to B = 2^(mn)
Empty relation R = φ; universal relation R = A × A (both are trivial relations)
traps: Don't count the pairs (mn) when asked for the number of relations (2^(mn))
Range is not the codomain: unused codomain elements are not in the range
Two elements sharing one image is still a function; one element with two images is not

topics.h: In a cricket team, 'is a teammate of' works both ways, but 'bats before' does not. Spotting such patterns is exactly what these three properties test.
p: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A. One missing (a, a) is enough to break it.
Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R for all a, b ∈ A.
Transitive: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R for all a, b, c ∈ A.
To disprove a property, one counter-example is enough. To prove it, argue for arbitrary elements.

Classic checks: '≤' on R is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric; 'is perpendicular to' (lines in a plane) is symmetric only; 'is parallel to' with each line counted parallel to itself is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

ex.q: On A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 3)}. Is R reflexive, symmetric, transitive?
st: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) are all in R, so R is reflexive.
(1, 2) ∈ R but (2, 1) ∉ R, so R is not symmetric.
(1, 2) and (2, 3) are in R but (1, 3) ∉ R, so R is not transitive.

topics.rl: Train connectivity in Indian Railways: if a direct train links Pune to Mumbai, one also links Mumbai to Pune (symmetric), but a direct Pune–Mumbai and Mumbai–Surat train does not guarantee a direct Pune–Surat train (not necessarily transitive).

rv.summary: A relation is reflexive if every a is related to itself, symmetric if (a, b) forces (b, a), and transitive if (a, b) and (b, c) force (a, c). One counter-example disproves a property.
focus: Test a given set of pairs for each property
Give a counter-example to show a property fails
Know the classic cases: ≤, perpendicular, parallel, divisibility
remember: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A
Transitive: (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R
traps: Don't call R reflexive if even one (a, a) is missing
(a, b), (b, a) ∈ R needs (a, a) for transitivity
Perpendicularity is symmetric only, not transitive

topics.h: A school splits 1200 students into houses. Each student is in exactly one house and no house overlaps another. That clean split is what an equivalence relation always produces.
p: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, all three together.
Congruence modulo n: on Z, a R b ⇔ n divides (a − b). It is always an equivalence relation.
Equivalence class [a] = {x ∈ A: x R a}, the set of all elements related to a.
Equivalence classes are pairwise disjoint and their union is the whole set: they partition A. Any two classes are either identical or disjoint.
Mod 2 on Z gives two classes (even and odd integers); mod n gives n classes [0], [1], …, [n − 1].

ex.q: A = {1, 2, …, 10}, R = {(a, b): |a − b| is a multiple of 4}. Find [1] and [2].
st: |a − a| = 0 is a multiple of 4, so R is reflexive; |a − b| = |b − a| makes it symmetric; if 4 | (a − b) and 4 | (b − c) then 4 | (a − c), so it is transitive.
[1] = elements x with x − 1 a multiple of 4: 1, 5, 9.
[2] = elements x with x − 2 a multiple of 4: 2, 6, 10.

topics.rl: In an RBI currency chest, notes are grouped by denomination: two notes are related if they have the same value. Each note sits in exactly one bundle, a perfect partition into equivalence classes.

rv.summary: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. It splits the set into equivalence classes that are disjoint and together make up the whole set.
focus: Check all three properties for a given relation
Find an equivalence class like [1] or [2]
Count classes for congruence modulo n
remember: Congruence mod n on Z has n classes [0], [1], …, [n − 1]
Two classes are either identical or disjoint
traps: Don't forget to check transitivity after reflexivity and symmetry
Classes never partly overlap: a common element means equal classes
The class of 1 under mod 2 is all odd integers, not just {1}

topics.h: Every Aadhaar number points to exactly one person, and no two people share a number. That 'no sharing' rule is what one-one means.
p: One-one (injective): different inputs give different outputs. Test: f(x1) = f(x2) ⇒ x1 = x2.
Many-one: some two different inputs share an output (e.g. f(x) = x² on R, f(−2) = f(2)).
Onto (surjective): every element of the codomain is an image, i.e. range = codomain. Test: for each y in codomain, solve y = f(x) and check x lies in the domain.
Bijective: one-one and onto both. Only bijections have inverse functions.
Changing the domain or codomain changes the answer: x² is one-one on N but not on R.

For a function from a finite set A to itself, one-one and onto go together: if f is one-one it is onto, and if onto it is one-one. This fails on infinite sets (f(x) = 2x on N is one-one but not onto).

ex.q: Show that f: R → R, f(x) = 3 − 4x is bijective.
st: Onto: let y ∈ R. Solve y = 3 − 4x: x = (3 − y)/4, which is a real number.
Then f((3 − y)/4) = 3 − (3 − y) = y, so every y has a pre-image.
ex.a: f is one-one and onto, hence bijective.

topics.rl: Seat allocation in a JEE exam centre must be one-one (no two candidates on one seat). If every seat is filled too, the allocation is a bijection between candidates and seats.

rv.summary: A function is one-one if different inputs give different outputs and onto if every codomain element is an image. A bijection is both, and the answer depends on the domain and codomain.
focus: Prove one-one using f(x1) = f(x2) ⇒ x1 = x2
Prove onto by solving y = f(x) and checking x is in the domain
Classify functions like 2x on N, x² on R, 1/x, x³
remember: On a finite set A → A, one-one ⇔ onto
traps: Don't use the finite-set rule on infinite sets: 2x on N is one-one but not onto
Don't give an onto reason when one-one is asked (and vice versa)
x² is one-one on N but not on R

topics.t: Standard and piecewise functions; counting functions
topics.h: A mobile plan that charges ₹199 up to 2 GB and more beyond is a piecewise function. Board papers love asking whether such functions are one-one or onto.
p: On R → R: modulus |x|, greatest integer [x] and signum function are neither one-one nor onto. x³ and ax + b (a ≠ 0) are bijective.
For piecewise functions, check each piece, then check that the pieces do not share outputs (for one-one) and together cover the codomain (for onto).
If n(A) = m and n(B) = n: number of functions A → B is nᵐ; number of one-one functions is n(n − 1)…(n − m + 1) when m ≤ n, and 0 when m > n.
Bijections from a set of n elements to itself: n!. Onto functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set: 2³ − 2 = 6.
Composition of functions, invertible functions and binary operations are not in the current CBSE syllabus.

ex.q: f: R → R, f(x) = 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, −1 if x < 0 (signum). Is f one-one? Onto?
st: f(1) = f(2) = 1, so f is not one-one.
2 in the codomain is not an image, so f is not onto.

topics.rl: Allotting 4 Olympiad medal designs to 4 toppers so each gets a different design can be done in 4! = 24 ways. That is counting bijections.

rv.summary: Modulus, greatest integer and signum functions on R are neither one-one nor onto, while x³ and ax + b (a ≠ 0) are bijective. Functions between finite sets can be counted with simple formulas.
focus: Classify |x|, [x], signum and piecewise functions
Count all, one-one, onto and bijective functions between finite sets
remember: One-one functions: n(n − 1)…(n − m + 1) if m ≤ n, else 0
Bijections of an n-element set to itself: n!
Onto functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set: 2³ − 2 = 6
traps: Don't count all functions when one-one functions are asked
If m > n there are 0 one-one functions
Don't forget to remove the constant functions when counting onto maps to a 2-element set

topics.t: Why restrict? sin⁻¹ x and cos⁻¹ x
topics.h: sin 30° = 1/2, but so do sin 150° and sin 390°. Ask a calculator for sin⁻¹(0.5) and it answers just 30°. Why that one? Because we cut sine down to a piece where it is one-one.
p: A function has an inverse only if it is one-one and onto (bijective).
sin x on R is many-one, so we restrict it to [−π/2, π/2] with codomain [−1, 1]. That gives sin⁻¹: [−1, 1] → [−π/2, π/2].
cos x is restricted to [0, π], giving cos⁻¹: [−1, 1] → [0, π].
These ranges are the principal value branches. y = sin⁻¹ x means sin y = x with y in [−π/2, π/2].
sin⁻¹ x is NOT (sin x)⁻¹. (sin x)⁻¹ = 1/sin x = cosec x.

ex.q: Find the domain of f(x) = sin⁻¹(2x − 1).

topics.rl: A ground station tracking a satellite can find its elevation angle from a sine ratio using sin⁻¹. The principal branch [−π/2, π/2] covers every angle from straight down to straight up, so the answer is never ambiguous.

rv.summary: Sine and cosine are many-one on R, so we restrict them to make them bijective. This gives sin⁻¹: [−1, 1] → [−π/2, π/2] and cos⁻¹: [−1, 1] → [0, π].
focus: State the domain and principal branch of sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹
Find the domain of expressions like sin⁻¹(2x − 1)
Explain why the restriction is needed
remember: y = sin⁻¹ x means sin y = x with y ∈ [−π/2, π/2]
traps: Don't read sin⁻¹ x as 1/sin x
Don't swap the sine branch [−π/2, π/2] with the cosine branch [0, π]
An input outside [−1, 1] is a domain problem, not a range problem

topics.t: tan⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹, cosec⁻¹ and the graphs
topics.h: A road sign says the gradient is 1 in 10. The angle of the slope is tan⁻¹(0.1). tan⁻¹ takes any real number at all, and it never reaches 90°.
p: tan⁻¹: R → (−π/2, π/2) and cot⁻¹: R → (0, π). Both have domain all real numbers.
The graph of an inverse function is the mirror image of the restricted function's graph in the line y = x (swap x and y).
sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ are increasing; cos⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ are decreasing. tan⁻¹ has horizontal asymptotes y = −π/2 and y = π/2.

ex.q: The point (π/6, 1/2) lies on y = sin x. Which point lies on y = sin⁻¹ x, and why?
st: The graph of sin⁻¹ is the reflection of the restricted sine graph in y = x.
Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates.
So (π/6, 1/2) becomes (1/2, π/6); indeed sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6.

topics.rl: A cricket ball hit with a launch slope m has launch angle tan⁻¹ m. Since tan⁻¹ is defined for every real m, a launch angle exists for any slope, however steep.

rv.summary: tan⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ accept every real number, while sec⁻¹ and cosec⁻¹ accept only |x| ≥ 1. The graph of each inverse is the mirror image of the restricted function in y = x.
focus: State domains and ranges of tan⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹, cosec⁻¹
Explain the excluded values 0 and π/2
Read points and asymptotes from the graphs
remember: tan⁻¹: R → (−π/2, π/2); cot⁻¹: R → (0, π)
Inverse graph = reflection in y = x
traps: Don't use the tan⁻¹ branch for cot⁻¹
Don't forget 0 is removed from the cosec⁻¹ range and π/2 from the sec⁻¹ range
cos⁻¹ is decreasing: its graph goes from (−1, π) to (1, 0)

topics.h: Board papers almost always have a 1- or 2-mark principal value question. The trap is always the same: a correct-looking angle from the wrong branch.
p: The principal value of an inverse trig function is its value in the principal branch.
Negative inputs: sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹ x, tan⁻¹(−x) = −tan⁻¹ x, cosec⁻¹(−x) = −cosec⁻¹ x.
But cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹ x, sec⁻¹(−x) = π − sec⁻¹ x, cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹ x.
Key values: sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6, cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3, tan⁻¹(1) = π/4, tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3, cos⁻¹(−1/2) = 2π/3.
For a sum, find each principal value first, then add.

ex.q: Find tan⁻¹(1) + cos⁻¹(−1/2) + sin⁻¹(−1/2).

topics.rl: Surveyors and civil engineers turn measured ratios (rise over run, height over distance) into angles with inverse trig. Agreeing to use the principal branch keeps everyone on the same answer.

rv.summary: A principal value is the value inside the principal branch. sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹ and cosec⁻¹ are odd, but cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ of −x equal π minus the value at x.
focus: Find principal values of negative inputs
Evaluate sums and differences of principal values
Reject angles outside the branch
remember: sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹ x; tan⁻¹(−x) = −tan⁻¹ x; cosec⁻¹(−x) = −cosec⁻¹ x
cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹ x; sec⁻¹(−x) = π − sec⁻¹ x; cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹ x
traps: Don't give a negative answer for cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹ or cot⁻¹
Don't treat cot⁻¹ as odd like tan⁻¹
An angle with the right sine (like 7π/6) is not the principal value unless it lies in the branch

topics.h: Is sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) equal to 2π/3? It looks obvious, and it is wrong. This topic shows why.
p: sin(sin⁻¹ x) = x for x ∈ [−1, 1], and sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only for x ∈ [−π/2, π/2]. Similar rules hold for cos (x ∈ [0, π]) and tan (x ∈ (−π/2, π/2)).
If the angle is outside the branch, rewrite it with the same sine/cos/tan value inside the branch: sin(2π/3) = sin(π/3), so sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) = π/3.
Substitutions simplify expressions: x = tan θ for 1 + x², x = sin θ or cos θ for 1 − x², x = sec θ for x² − 1.
Useful identities: 2 tan⁻¹ x = sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) for |x| ≤ 1, and tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)) for |x| < 1.
The formal properties section of this chapter is not in the current CBSE syllabus; domains, ranges, principal values, graphs and these worked simplifications are examined.

ex.q: Write tan⁻¹[(√(1 + x²) − 1)/x], x ≠ 0, in simplest form.
st: Put x = tan θ, θ ∈ (−π/2, π/2), θ ≠ 0. Then √(1 + x²) = sec θ.
θ/2 lies in (−π/4, π/4), so tan⁻¹(tan θ/2) = θ/2 = (1/2) tan⁻¹ x.

topics.rl: Robotics teams in IIT tech fests convert sensor ratios to joint angles with inverse trig. If the arm's angle can go beyond the principal branch, they must shift it back, exactly like sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) = π/3.

rv.summary: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only when x is in the branch; otherwise rewrite the angle inside the branch first. Substitutions such as x = tan θ or x = a sin θ reduce expressions to simplest form.
focus: Evaluate sin⁻¹(sin x), cos⁻¹(cos x) for angles outside the branch
Simplify expressions with x = tan θ, sin θ, sec θ substitutions
Evaluate nested expressions step by step
remember: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only for x ∈ [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹(cos x) = x only for x ∈ [0, π]
1 + x² → x = tan θ; a² − x² → x = a sin θ; x² − 1 → x = sec θ
traps: Don't cancel sin⁻¹ and sin without checking the branch
Don't use x = a tan θ for a² − x²
Check the half angle lies in the branch before the last step

topics.t: What is a matrix? Order and construction
topics.h: Every IPL scorecard is a grid: rows for batters, columns for runs, balls, fours and sixes. Mathematicians call such a grid a matrix and can do algebra with it.
p: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers (or functions) in rows and columns. The element in row i and column j is aij.
A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m × n and has mn elements.
For a given number of elements N, the possible orders are all factor pairs: each divisor d of N gives the order d × (N/d).
A matrix can be built from a rule aij = f(i, j) by plugging in each i and j.
Matrices store data (sales, marks) and coordinates of points of a figure compactly; they also make systems of equations easy to handle.

ex.q: Construct a 2 × 3 matrix with aij = 2i − j.

topics.rl: A dairy cooperative tracking milk, butter and paneer sales in four cities each month can store them as a 3 × 4 matrix; adding the monthly matrices gives the yearly totals in one step.

rv.summary: A matrix is a rectangular array; with m rows and n columns its order is m × n and it has mn elements. Entries can be built from a rule aij = f(i, j).
focus: Read an element aij (row i, column j)
Count the possible orders for N elements
Construct a matrix from a rule like aij = 2i − j
remember: Order m × n = rows × columns; number of elements = mn
Possible orders for N elements = number of divisors of N
Row matrix: 1 × n; column matrix: m × 1
traps: Don't write columns × rows for the order
4 × 6 and 6 × 4 are different orders; count both
Don't drop the modulus or a factor like /2 in the rule

topics.h: Identity matrices are the '1' of matrix algebra and zero matrices are the '0'. Knowing the family names saves marks in every board paper.
p: Row matrix: 1 × n. Column matrix: m × 1. Square matrix: m = n; its diagonal elements are a11, a22, …, ann.
Diagonal matrix: square, all non-diagonal elements zero. Scalar matrix: diagonal with all diagonal elements equal.
Identity matrix I: scalar matrix with every diagonal element 1. Zero (null) matrix O: every element 0 (any order).
Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and every corresponding element is equal.
Equality lets you set up equations: equate entries one by one and solve.
topics.rl: A scalar matrix like 5I scales every coordinate by 5, the same way a zoom on Google Maps of India scales every distance by the same factor.

rv.summary: Special matrices include row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity and zero matrices. Two matrices are equal only if they have the same order and equal corresponding entries.
focus: Identify the type of a given matrix
Solve for unknowns by equating corresponding entries
Know which types contain which (identity ⊂ scalar ⊂ diagonal)
remember: Scalar matrix: diagonal with all diagonal entries equal
Identity I: scalar with every diagonal entry 1
Equal matrices: same order and every aij = bij
traps: Not every diagonal matrix is scalar, and not every scalar matrix is I
A zero matrix need not be square
Matrices with the same entries but different orders are not equal

topics.h: Two branches of a Kirana chain each record sales in a matrix. Add the matrices and you get the combined sales in one stroke.
p: A + B is defined only when A and B have the same order; add corresponding elements.
kA multiplies every element by k. −A = (−1)A and A − B = A + (−B).
Addition is commutative (A + B = B + A) and associative; O is the additive identity and −A is the additive inverse.
Scalar rules: k(A + B) = kA + kB, (k + l)A = kA + lA.
Solve matrix equations like ordinary ones: from 2A + 3X = 5B, X = (1/3)(5B − 2A).
topics.rl: A Delhi electronics shop stores stock as a matrix. A festive restock adds one matrix; a Diwali discount of 10% is the scalar multiple 0.9 × (price matrix).

rv.summary: Matrices of the same order are added entry by entry, and kA multiplies every entry by k. Matrix equations like 2A + 3X = 5B are solved just like ordinary equations.
focus: Compute A + B, A − B and kA
Solve pairs like X + Y = P, X − Y = Q
Know when a sum is defined
remember: A + B defined only for the same order
k(A + B) = kA + kB; (k + l)A = kA + lA
traps: Don't add matrices of different orders
Divide by 2 after adding X + Y and X − Y
Subtract in the right order to get Y, not −Y

topics.h: Multiply a row of quantities by a column of prices and you get the bill. That is matrix multiplication, and it powers everything from shopping carts to Google search.
p: AB is defined when columns of A = rows of B. If A is m × n and B is n × p, AB is m × p.
Row-by-column rule: (AB)ik = ai1 b1k + ai2 b2k + … + ain bnk.
AB ≠ BA in general; one may even be undefined. AB = O is possible with A ≠ O and B ≠ O.
Associative: (AB)C = A(BC). Distributive: A(B + C) = AB + AC. Identity: AI = IA = A.
To verify identities like A² − 5A + 7I = O, compute A², then combine entry by entry.

ex.q: If A = [[3, 1], [−1, 2]], show that A² − 5A + 7I = O.

topics.rl: A school in Jaipur buys 3 pens at ₹10 each, 5 notebooks at ₹40 each and 2 geometry boxes at ₹25 each: the bill [3 5 2] × [10; 40; 25] = 30 + 200 + 50 = ₹280 is one matrix product.

rv.summary: AB is defined when the columns of A equal the rows of B, and each entry is a row-by-column sum. Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive but not commutative.
focus: Compute entries of AB by the row-by-column rule
Find the order of a product
Verify identities like A² − 5A + 7I = O
remember: (AB)ik = ai1 b1k + ai2 b2k + … + ain bnk
AB ≠ BA in general; AB = O is possible with A, B ≠ O
traps: Don't multiply entry by entry
(A + B)² is not A² + 2AB + B² unless AB = BA
Don't confuse AB with BA when asked for one of them

topics.h: A distance table between Indian cities reads the same across and down: Delhi to Agra equals Agra to Delhi. That table is a symmetric matrix.
p: The transpose A′ (or Aᵀ) is formed by turning rows into columns. If A is m × n, A′ is n × m.
Properties: (A′)′ = A, (kA)′ = kA′, (A + B)′ = A′ + B′, (AB)′ = B′A′ (order reverses).
Symmetric: A′ = A (aij = aji). Skew-symmetric: A′ = −A (aij = −aji), so every diagonal element is 0.
For any square A: A + A′ is symmetric and A − A′ is skew-symmetric.
Every square matrix is uniquely A = (1/2)(A + A′) + (1/2)(A − A′), a symmetric plus a skew-symmetric matrix.

ex.q: Express A = [[3, 5], [1, −1]] as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.

topics.rl: A table of road distances between cities is a symmetric matrix (Delhi to Agra equals Agra to Delhi), which is why such charts are often printed as only half a table.

rv.summary: The transpose A′ turns rows into columns. A is symmetric if A′ = A and skew-symmetric if A′ = −A, and every square matrix is a symmetric part plus a skew-symmetric part.
focus: Use transpose rules, especially (AB)′ = B′A′
Find missing entries of symmetric or skew-symmetric matrices
remember: Symmetric: aij = aji; skew-symmetric: aij = −aji, diagonal all 0
traps: Don't forget the factor 1/2 in the parts
Use A − A′, not A′ − A, for the skew part
Don't transpose a product without reversing the order

topics.h: Dividing by a number means multiplying by its reciprocal. Matrices have no division, but some have an inverse that does the same job.
p: A square matrix A is invertible if there is B with AB = BA = I. Then B = A⁻¹.
The inverse, if it exists, is unique: if B and C are both inverses, B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C.
(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹: the order reverses, just like a transpose of a product.
Only square matrices can have inverses (but not every square matrix has one).
Finding inverses by elementary row or column operations is not in the current syllabus; Chapter 4 gives the adjoint method.

ex.q: Show that B = [[1, −1], [−1, 2]] is the inverse of A = [[2, 1], [1, 1]].

topics.rl: Old-school codes like the Hill cipher scramble a message by multiplying with a matrix; the receiver unscrambles it with the inverse matrix.

rv.summary: A square matrix A is invertible if some B gives AB = BA = I; this inverse is unique. The inverse of a product reverses the order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.
focus: Verify that B is the inverse of A
Use (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ and uniqueness
Find A⁻¹ from a matrix equation like A² − 3A + I = O
remember: Only square matrices can have inverses
traps: Don't take reciprocals of entries (except for a diagonal matrix)
Don't write (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹
Not every square matrix has an inverse

topics.h: Every square matrix carries one secret number, its determinant. That single number tells you whether a system of equations has a unique solution.
p: The determinant |A| (or det A) is defined only for square matrices. For A = [a], |A| = a.
3 × 3: expand along any row or column, e.g. along R1: a11(a22a33 − a23a32) − a12(a21a33 − a23a31) + a13(a21a32 − a22a31).
Signs follow the chessboard pattern + − + / − + − / + − +. Every row or column gives the same value.
Smart move: expand along the row or column with the most zeros.

st: Row 2 has two zeros, so expand along R2.
Only a23 = −1 survives; its sign position is (−1)^(2+3) = −1.

topics.rl: Engineers who solve structural load equations check the determinant first: a zero determinant warns them that the system has no unique solution.

rv.summary: A determinant is a number defined only for a square matrix: ad − bc for 2 × 2, and expansion along any row or column for 3 × 3. Expanding along the row or column with most zeros saves work.
focus: Evaluate 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 determinants by expansion
Use the chessboard sign pattern correctly
Choose the row or column with most zeros
remember: Every row or column gives the same value
traps: Don't forget the − sign on the middle term of a row-1 expansion
Only square matrices have determinants
Watch double negatives like −(−sin θ)(sin θ)

topics.t: det(kA), determinant equations and trig entries
topics.h: Double every entry of a 3 × 3 matrix and the determinant does not double: it becomes eight times bigger. Here is why.
p: For an n × n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|, because each of the n rows is multiplied by k.
To solve |…x…| = |…|, expand both sides and solve the resulting equation (often a quadratic).
With trigonometric entries, expand and then use identities like sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
The formal 'properties of determinants' section is not in the current CBSE syllabus, so evaluate by expansion.
topics.rl: Scaling a map of the Western Ghats by 2 in each direction scales areas by 2² = 4. A determinant measures that area factor, so |2A| = 4|A| for a 2 × 2 matrix.

rv.summary: For an n × n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|. Determinant equations are solved by expanding both sides, and trig entries simplify with identities like sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
focus: Find |kA| for 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 matrices
Solve equations where both sides are determinants
Simplify determinants with trig entries
traps: Don't write |kA| = k|A|
x² = 36 gives x = ±6, not 36
Take care with a negative entry: 6·3 − (−2)(7) = 18 + 14

topics.t: Area of a triangle and collinearity
topics.h: Three GPS pins on a farm in Punjab: what area do they enclose? A 3 × 3 determinant answers in one line.
p: Area of triangle with vertices (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) = (1/2)|Δ|, where Δ = |[[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|.
Area is always positive, so take the absolute value of Δ.
The points are collinear exactly when Δ = 0 (zero area).
Equation of the line through (x1, y1) and (x2, y2): |[[x, y, 1], [x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1]]| = 0.
If the area is given, (1/2)|Δ| = area gives two cases, Δ = +2·area or −2·area, so usually two answers.

ex.q: Find k if the area of the triangle with vertices (k, 0), (4, 0), (0, 2) is 4 square units.

topics.rl: Under the SVAMITVA scheme, village house plots are mapped with drone surveys. Once a plot's corner coordinates are known, its area can be found with the 'shoelace' formula, which is this determinant idea extended to polygons.

rv.summary: The area of a triangle is (1/2)|Δ| where Δ is the determinant of the vertex coordinates with a column of 1s. The points are collinear exactly when Δ = 0.
focus: Find the area of a triangle from its vertices
Find k for collinearity or for a given area
Write the line through two points as a determinant
traps: Don't forget the factor 1/2
Area is positive: take the absolute value
Don't drop the negative case when area is given

topics.h: Cover one row and one column of a determinant and a smaller determinant is left. That leftover, with a sign, is the building block of inverses.
p: Minor Mij: the determinant left after deleting row i and column j.
Cofactor Aij = (−1)^(i+j) Mij. The sign is + when i + j is even and − when it is odd.
Δ = sum of (elements of any row or column) × (their own cofactors): Δ = a11A11 + a12A12 + a13A13.
Elements of one row times cofactors of a DIFFERENT row always add to 0, e.g. a11A21 + a12A22 + a13A23 = 0.
For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]]: A11 = d, A12 = −c, A21 = −b, A22 = a.
topics.rl: Cofactors give a quick formula for inverting small 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 matrices, like the ones computer graphics uses to rotate and resize 3D models.

rv.summary: The minor Mij is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j, and the cofactor is Aij = (−1)^(i+j) Mij. A row times its own cofactors gives Δ; times another row's cofactors gives 0.
focus: Find minors and cofactors of 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 matrices
Expand Δ using cofactors
Know the zero-sum result for a different row
traps: Don't give the minor when the cofactor is asked
Positions with i + j odd carry a minus sign
A different row's cofactors give 0, not Δ

topics.t: Adjoint and inverse of a matrix
topics.h: To undo a matrix you need its inverse, and the adjoint is the recipe: cofactors, a transpose, and one division by |A|.
p: adj A is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. For [[a, b], [c, d]]: adj = [[d, −b], [−c, a]] (swap the diagonal, negate the others).
A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I.
A is singular if |A| = 0 and non-singular if |A| ≠ 0. |AB| = |A||B|.
A is invertible ⇔ A is non-singular, and then A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A.
If A² + aA + bI = O with b ≠ 0, multiply by A⁻¹: A + aI + bA⁻¹ = O, so A⁻¹ = −(1/b)(A + aI).

ex.q: Find the inverse of A = [[2, 3], [1, −4]].

topics.rl: Rotation matrices, used to switch a satellite's or a drone camera's view from one coordinate frame to another, always have determinant 1, so their inverses always exist.

rv.summary: adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix and A(adj A) = |A| I. A is invertible only when |A| ≠ 0, and then A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A.
focus: Write adj A for a 2 × 2 matrix quickly
Find A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A
Use |AB| = |A||B| and matrix equations to find A⁻¹
traps: Singular (|A| = 0) matrices have no inverse
Divide by |A| including its sign
Don't add determinants for |AB|

topics.t: Solving linear equations by the matrix method
topics.h: Three unknown prices, three bills. Write them as AX = B, and one inverse matrix solves the lot.
p: A system is consistent if it has at least one solution, and inconsistent if it has none.
Write the system as AX = B, where A holds the coefficients, X the unknowns and B the constants.
If |A| ≠ 0, the unique solution is X = A⁻¹B.
If |A| = 0, find (adj A)B. If (adj A)B ≠ O, the system is inconsistent. If (adj A)B = O, it may be consistent with infinitely many solutions or inconsistent; check the equations.
If a product like AB = kI is given, then A⁻¹ = (1/k)B, which saves computing cofactors.

ex.q: Solve x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2, 2x + y − z = 1 by the matrix method.
st: |A| = 1(1 − 1) − 1(−1 − 2) + 1(1 + 2) = 6 ≠ 0, so there is a unique solution.
Computing X = A⁻¹B gives x = 1, y = 2, z = 3.

topics.rl: A Pune bakery's three outlets sell three cake types. Knowing each outlet's total sales and quantities, the owner finds each cake's price with X = A⁻¹B.

rv.summary: Write a linear system as AX = B. If |A| ≠ 0 the unique solution is X = A⁻¹B; if |A| = 0, check (adj A)B to decide between no solution and infinitely many.
focus: Solve 2 and 3 variable systems by X = A⁻¹B
Decide consistency when |A| = 0
Form equations from word problems
remember: |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = O ⇒ infinitely many or none; check the equations
traps: |A| = 0 does not always mean infinitely many solutions
Don't report y when x is asked
Keep the sign of |A| when dividing

topics.h: Draw the graph of a train's distance from Delhi without lifting your pen: no train teleports, so distance is a continuous function of time.
p: Intuitively, f is continuous at x = c if its graph has no break, jump or hole there.
Formally: f is continuous at c if f(c) is defined and lim(x→c) f(x) = f(c), i.e. LHL = RHL = f(c).
If this fails, c is a point of discontinuity (only points in the domain are tested).
f is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it; a continuous function is continuous at every point of its domain.
The greatest integer function [x] is discontinuous at every integer: just left of 2 it is 1, at 2 it is 2.

ex.q: Is f(x) = x + 2 for x ≤ 1 and x − 2 for x > 1 continuous at x = 1?
st: LHL ≠ RHL, so the limit does not exist.
ex.a: Not continuous at x = 1 (it has a jump).

topics.rl: Mobile data billing in slabs (₹ per GB jumping at 2 GB, 5 GB) is a step function like [x]: the bill jumps, so it is discontinuous at each slab boundary.

rv.summary: f is continuous at c when f(c) is defined and LHL = RHL = f(c), so the graph has no break, jump or hole there. The greatest integer function breaks at every integer.
focus: Find LHL, RHL and f(c) for piecewise functions
Decide continuity at a junction or a removable point
Know where [x] is discontinuous
remember: Continuous at c ⇔ lim(x→c⁻) f = lim(x→c⁺) f = f(c)
traps: Equal one-sided limits are not enough; they must also equal f(c)
Use the correct piece for each side of the junction
Defining a value at a bad point does not remove a jump or blow-up

topics.h: Boards love a 3-mark question: 'Find k so that f is continuous.' It is just two limits set equal, and here you master it.
p: Constant, identity, polynomial, modulus, sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere; rational functions and tan x are continuous on their domains.
If f and g are continuous at c, so are f + g, f − g, fg and f/g (when g(c) ≠ 0).
A composition of continuous functions is continuous: |sin x|, sin(x²), cos|x|, e^(sin x).
For a piecewise function, the only doubtful points are the junctions; check LHL = RHL = f(c) there.
To find unknown constants, equate the left and right values at each junction and solve.

ex.q: Find k so that f(x) = kx + 1 (x ≤ 5) and 3x − 5 (x > 5) is continuous at x = 5.

topics.rl: Highway engineers join a straight road to a curved ramp. The two formulas must give the same height at the joint, the same 'equate both sides' step that finds k.

rv.summary: Polynomials, |x|, sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere, and sums, products, quotients (non-zero denominator) and compositions keep continuity. Unknown constants come from LHL = RHL = f(c) at junctions.
focus: Find constants that make a piecewise function continuous
Use algebra and composition of continuous functions
Check only the junctions of piecewise functions
remember: f ± g, fg continuous; f/g continuous when g(c) ≠ 0
Composition of continuous functions is continuous
traps: Don't forget to square: kx² at x = 2 gives 4k
A constant multiplying zero (λ · 0) cannot fix a gap
Not every junction is a discontinuity

topics.h: A V-shaped graph has no break but has a sharp corner. Continuous, yes. Differentiable, no. That one corner hides a whole idea.
p: f is differentiable at c if the left and right derivatives lim(h→0) [f(c + h) − f(c)]/h are equal and finite.
Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but continuous does not imply differentiable: |x| is continuous at 0 but has no derivative there.
Standard rules from Class XI: (u ± v)′ = u′ ± v′, (uv)′ = u′v + uv′, (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v².
Chain rule: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). Differentiate the outside, keep the inside, multiply by the inside's derivative.
[x] is not differentiable at integers (not even continuous); |x − 1| is not differentiable at x = 1.

ex.q: Differentiate y = sin(x²).
st: Outer function: sin u, with u = x².
d/du (sin u) = cos u, and du/dx = 2x.

topics.rl: Mission control tracks a rocket's height h(t) and its vertical speed v(t) = h′(t). Speed is a derivative, and the chain rule converts rates when altitude depends on time through another variable.

rv.summary: f is differentiable at c when the left and right derivatives are equal and finite; differentiability implies continuity, but not the reverse. The chain rule differentiates the outside, keeps the inside, and multiplies by the inside's derivative.
focus: Apply the chain rule to multi-layer functions
Find left and right derivatives of |x| type functions
Locate points where a function is not differentiable
remember: |x − a| has a corner (not differentiable) at x = a
traps: Don't stop the chain rule after one layer
Don't reverse the implication between continuity and differentiability
|x| is continuous at 0 even though it is not differentiable there

topics.t: Implicit functions and inverse trig derivatives
topics.h: x² + xy + y² = 100 is an oval, not a formula for y. You can still find its slope at any point, without ever solving for y.
p: Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x, so d/dx(y²) = 2y dy/dx and d/dx(xy) = y + x dy/dx. Then solve for dy/dx.
d/dx (sin⁻¹ x) = 1/√(1 − x²) and d/dx (cos⁻¹ x) = −1/√(1 − x²), for −1 < x < 1.
d/dx (tan⁻¹ x) = 1/(1 + x²) for all real x.
Simplify before differentiating: with x = tan θ, sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) = 2 tan⁻¹ x for |x| < 1, so its derivative is 2/(1 + x²).
Similarly, tan⁻¹[(3x − x³)/(1 − 3x²)] = 3 tan⁻¹ x for |x| < 1/√3.

ex.q: Find dy/dx if x² + xy + y² = 100.

topics.rl: Car and product designers describe smooth body curves by equations in x and y; implicit differentiation gives the slope of such a curve at any point without solving for y.

rv.summary: For implicit equations, differentiate both sides treating y as a function of x and solve for dy/dx. Inverse trig derivatives are often easiest after a substitution like x = tan θ or x = sin θ.
focus: Find dy/dx for implicit curves like x² + y² = 25 or xy = 12
Use the derivatives of sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹
Simplify inverse trig expressions before differentiating
remember: d/dx(y²) = 2y y′; d/dx(xy) = y + x y′
traps: Don't forget the − sign in the derivative of cos⁻¹ x
For a circle y′ = −x/y; for xy = c it is −y/x
Keep the chain factor, e.g. (tan⁻¹ 2x)′ = 2/(1 + 4x²)

topics.h: Your SIP grows exponentially and the Richter scale uses logarithms. Calculus treats both with two beautifully simple rules.
p: Exponential function bˣ (b > 0, b ≠ 1): domain R, range (0, ∞), passes through (0, 1). The most important base is e ≈ 2.718.
logₐ x is the inverse of aˣ: logₐ x = y ⇔ aʸ = x, defined for x > 0. log x (natural log) means base e in this chapter.
Laws: log(pq) = log p + log q, log(p/q) = log p − log q, log(pⁿ) = n log p, change of base: logₐ p = log p / log a.
d/dx (eˣ) = eˣ and d/dx (log x) = 1/x for x > 0.
With the chain rule: d/dx e^(f(x)) = f′(x) e^(f(x)) and d/dx log f(x) = f′(x)/f(x).

ex.q: Differentiate y = log(cos eˣ).
st: Outer: log u with u = cos eˣ, so dy/du = 1/cos eˣ.

topics.rl: The pH scale used in chemistry labs is −log₁₀[H⁺]: each step down in pH means ten times more hydrogen ions, a logarithm at work.

rv.summary: eˣ is its own derivative and log x (base e, x > 0) has derivative 1/x. With the chain rule, e^(f(x)) gives f′(x)e^(f(x)) and log f(x) gives f′(x)/f(x).
focus: Differentiate e^(f(x)) and log f(x)
Use the laws of logarithms and change of base
Know the domain and range of eˣ and log x
remember: log(pq) = log p + log q; log pⁿ = n log p
logₐ p = log p / log a
log x is defined only for x > 0
traps: log of a product is a sum, not a product of logs
Don't include 0 in the domain of log x
Don't bring the exponent down in e^(f(x)) as if it were a power

topics.h: How do you differentiate xˣ? The power rule fails and the exponential rule fails. Take a log first, and the problem melts.
p: For y = u(x)^v(x), take logs: log y = v log u. Differentiate implicitly: (1/y) dy/dx = v′ log u + v u′/u.
So dy/dx = u^v [v′ log u + v u′/u]. Example: d/dx (xˣ) = xˣ(1 + log x).
Long products and quotients: log y = sum of logs turns products into sums, which are easy to differentiate.
aˣ = e^(x log a), so d/dx (aˣ) = aˣ log a.
Equations like xʸ = yˣ: take logs (y log x = x log y), then differentiate implicitly.

ex.q: Differentiate y = x^(sin x), x > 0.
st: log y = sin x · log x.
(1/y) dy/dx = cos x · log x + sin x · (1/x).
ex.a: dy/dx = x^(sin x) [cos x log x + (sin x)/x]

topics.rl: Economists measure growth rates and elasticities with logarithms, since d(log y) = dy/y is the relative (percentage) change in y.

rv.summary: When both base and exponent vary, or for long products and quotients, take logs first and differentiate implicitly. This gives d/dx(xˣ) = xˣ(1 + log x) and d/dx(aˣ) = aˣ log a.
focus: Differentiate u(x)^v(x) by taking logs
Handle products and quotients with log y
Solve equations like xʸ = yˣ for dy/dx
remember: dy/dx = u^v [v′ log u + v u′/u]
traps: Don't use the power rule on xˣ or on 3ˣ
Denominator factors give minus terms after taking logs
Don't forget the product rule on y log x

topics.h: A point on a bicycle tyre traces a cycloid. Its x and y each depend on the angle turned. To find the slope, let the angle do the work.
p: A curve can be given by x = f(t), y = g(t), where t is a parameter.
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0.
Parabola x = at², y = 2at: dy/dx = 2a/(2at) = 1/t.
Ellipse x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ: dy/dx = (b cos θ)/(−a sin θ) = −(b/a) cot θ.
Astroid x = a cos³θ, y = a sin³θ: dy/dx = −tan θ. Cycloid x = a(θ − sin θ), y = a(1 + cos θ): dy/dx = −cot(θ/2).

ex.q: Find dy/dx if x = a cos³θ and y = a sin³θ.
st: dy/dx = (3a sin²θ cos θ)/(−3a cos²θ sin θ) = −sin θ/cos θ.

topics.rl: A cricket ball's flight is tracked by Hawk-Eye as x(t) and y(t). Its direction at any instant is dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

rv.summary: For a curve x = f(t), y = g(t), dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt) as long as dx/dt ≠ 0. Standard results: parabola 1/t, ellipse −(b/a) cot θ, astroid −tan θ, cycloid −cot(θ/2).
focus: Find dy/dx in parametric form
Evaluate dy/dx at a given t or θ
Simplify answers with trig identities
remember: x = a cos³θ, y = a sin³θ ⇒ dy/dx = −tan θ
traps: Don't divide dx/dt by dy/dt
Don't lose the minus sign from d(cos θ)
No need to eliminate t first

topics.h: Velocity is the first derivative of position; acceleration is the second. Second derivatives tell you how fast the change itself is changing.
p: The second derivative d²y/dx² = d/dx(dy/dx), also written y″, y₂ or f″(x).
Explicit functions: just differentiate twice. y = sin x gives y″ = −sin x.
Implicit: differentiate the expression for y′ again, then substitute y′.
Parametric: d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)] ÷ (dx/dt), not (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²).
Typical proofs: y = A cos x + B sin x ⇒ y″ + y = 0; y = sin⁻¹ x ⇒ (1 − x²)y″ − xy′ = 0. (Rolle's theorem and the Mean Value Theorem are not in the current syllabus.)

ex.q: If y = sin⁻¹ x, show that (1 − x²) y″ − x y′ = 0.
st: Multiply by √(1 − x²): (1 − x²) y″ − x y′ = 0.

topics.rl: At the Buddh circuit, a racing car's speedometer shows the first derivative of distance, while the g-force sensor measures the second derivative, acceleration.

rv.summary: The second derivative is the derivative of dy/dx. For parametric curves, d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)] ÷ (dx/dt), and for implicit curves you differentiate y′ again and substitute.
focus: Find y″ for explicit, implicit and parametric functions
Prove relations like y″ + y = 0 or x²y″ + xy′ + y = 0
remember: y = A cos x + B sin x ⇒ y″ + y = 0
traps: d²y/dx² is not (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²)
Use the chain rule on sec²x and the product rule on xy′
Don't stop at the first derivative

topics.h: Drop a pebble in a pond: the ripple's radius grows at a steady 5 cm/s, but its area grows faster and faster. Derivatives tell you exactly how fast.
p: Derivatives help us study rates of change, where functions rise or fall, and their highest and lowest values.
dy/dx is the rate of change of y with respect to x; its value at x = x₀ is the rate at that instant.
If x and y both depend on t, then dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt), and dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
Circle: A = πr², dA/dr = 2πr. Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, dV/dr = 4πr²; S = 4πr², dS/dr = 8πr.
Cube of edge x: V = x³, dV/dt = 3x² dx/dt; S = 6x², dS/dt = 12x dx/dt. Cone: V = (1/3)πr²h.

ex.q: The volume of a cube increases at 9 cm³/s. How fast is its surface area increasing when an edge is 10 cm?
st: V = x³ ⇒ dV/dt = 3x² dx/dt ⇒ 9 = 3(100) dx/dt ⇒ dx/dt = 3/100 cm/s.

topics.rl: During the monsoon, dam engineers estimate how fast a reservoir's water level is rising from the rate of inflow, a classic related-rates calculation.

rv.summary: dy/dx measures how fast y changes with x, and when both depend on time, dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). Use the standard area and volume formulas for circles, spheres and cubes.
focus: Find the rate of change of area or volume at an instant
Use the chain rule with time rates like dr/dt
Work backwards from a given rate to find another
traps: Don't forget to multiply by dx/dt (or dr/dt)
Don't give the volume or area instead of its rate
Keep the factor 2 from d(r²)/dr = 2r

topics.t: Related rates in action; marginal cost and revenue
topics.h: A ladder slides down a wall; sand piles into a cone; a factory adds one more unit. Each is one equation, differentiated with respect to time or quantity.
p: Strategy: draw a diagram, name variables, write an equation linking them, differentiate with respect to t, then substitute the given values.
Ladder of length L: x² + y² = L² ⇒ x dx/dt + y dy/dt = 0.
Use a fixed ratio (like h = r/6 in a sand cone) to reduce to one variable before differentiating.
Marginal cost MC = dC/dx: approximate cost of producing one more unit. Marginal revenue MR = dR/dx.
A negative rate means the quantity is decreasing, e.g. the top of the ladder moving down.

ex.q: A 5 m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is pulled away at 2 cm/s. How fast does the top slide down when the foot is 4 m from the wall?
st: 4(2) + 3 dy/dt = 0 ⇒ dy/dt = −8/3 cm/s (units of the rate stay cm/s).
ex.a: The top slides down at 8/3 cm/s.

topics.rl: An Indian textile mill uses marginal cost to decide whether producing one more batch of cotton fabric will add more to cost than to revenue.

rv.summary: For related rates, link the variables by one equation, differentiate with respect to time and substitute values. Marginal cost and marginal revenue are dC/dx and dR/dx.
focus: Ladder, shadow, cone and balloon problems
Find marginal cost and marginal revenue at a given output
Interpret the sign of a rate
remember: A negative rate means the quantity is decreasing
traps: Don't compute C(x) or R(x) when the marginal value is asked
Use the correct ratio (r = 6h, not h = 6r) before differentiating
For shadows, the big triangle's base is x + s

topics.h: A Sensex chart rises and falls. Where it climbs, its slope is positive; where it dips, negative. The sign of f′ is the whole story.
p: f is increasing on I if x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) ≤ f(x2); strictly increasing if x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) < f(x2). Decreasing and strictly decreasing are defined similarly.
f is increasing at x₀ if it is increasing on some open interval around x₀.
If f′(x) > 0 on (a, b), f is strictly increasing on [a, b] (f continuous on [a, b]). If f′(x) < 0, strictly decreasing.
If f′(x) = 0 throughout, f is constant.
A constant function is both increasing and decreasing (not strictly).

ex.q: Show that f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 4x is strictly increasing on R.
ex.a: f′(x) > 0 for all x, so f is strictly increasing on R.

topics.rl: A home-loan EMI is an increasing function of the interest rate: for the same loan amount and tenure, a higher rate always means a higher EMI.

rv.summary: If f′(x) > 0 on an interval, f is strictly increasing there; if f′(x) < 0, strictly decreasing; if f′ = 0 throughout, constant. A single zero of f′ (like x³ at 0) does not stop strict increase.
focus: Decide if a function is increasing or decreasing on an interval
Use the sign of f′ for standard functions
Know what 'increasing at a point' means
remember: Strictly increasing: x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) < f(x2)
traps: Don't forget the minus sign in the derivatives of cos x and e^(−x)
x² is neither increasing nor decreasing at 0
log x lives only on (0, ∞)

topics.t: Finding intervals of increase and decrease
topics.h: Board paper favourite: 'Find the intervals in which f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 36x + 7 is increasing.' One factorisation, one sign chart, full marks.
p: Step 1: find f′(x) and solve f′(x) = 0 (also note where f′ is undefined). These points split the line into intervals.
Step 2: test the sign of f′ in each interval. Positive ⇒ increasing, negative ⇒ decreasing.
Write answers with intervals: strictly increasing on (−∞, −2) ∪ (3, ∞) style.
For trigonometric functions, work inside the given interval, e.g. [0, 2π].
To find a constant that makes f increasing on an interval, require f′(x) ≥ 0 throughout it.

ex.q: Find the intervals in which f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 36x + 7 is strictly increasing or decreasing.
ex.a: Strictly increasing on (−∞, −2) and (3, ∞); strictly decreasing on (−2, 3).

topics.rl: Transport planners model fuel cost against vehicle speed; finding where the cost function rises or falls shows which speed range is wasteful.

rv.summary: To find intervals of increase or decrease, solve f′(x) = 0, split the line at those points, and test the sign of f′ in each interval.
focus: Factorise f′ and draw a sign chart
Write answers as intervals
Find a constant that makes f increasing on an interval
remember: Points where f′ = 0 or f′ is undefined split the intervals
traps: Don't ignore a negative leading coefficient when reading signs
Don't include points outside the domain, like x = 0 for 2/x
For trig functions, stay inside the given interval

topics.t: Local maxima, minima and the first derivative test
topics.h: A trekker on the Western Ghats reaches a peak: just before it the path climbs, just after it falls. That sign change is the first derivative test.
p: f has a local maximum at c if f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x near c; a local minimum if f(c) ≤ f(x) near c. The largest value over the whole domain is the (absolute) maximum value.
Critical points: c in the domain where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist. Local extrema can occur only at critical points.
First derivative test: f′ changes + to − at c ⇒ local maximum; − to + ⇒ local minimum.
If f′ does not change sign at c (like x³ at 0), c is neither: it is a point of inflection.
Some extrema need no calculus: (2x − 1)² + 3 has minimum 3 since a square is ≥ 0; sin 2x + 5 lies between 4 and 6.

ex.q: Find the local maxima and minima of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 15.
st: At x = 1, f′ changes from + to −: local maximum f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 15 = 19.
At x = 3, f′ changes from − to +: local minimum f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 + 15 = 15.
ex.a: Local max 19 at x = 1; local min 15 at x = 3.

topics.rl: Farm scientists look for the fertiliser dose at which crop yield peaks: the slope of the yield curve changes from positive to negative there.

rv.summary: Local extrema occur only at critical points, where f′ = 0 or f′ does not exist. By the first derivative test, f′ changing + to − gives a local maximum and − to + a local minimum.
focus: Find critical points, including corners
Apply the first derivative test
Find local maximum and minimum values
remember: Critical point: f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) undefined
+ to − ⇒ local max; − to + ⇒ local min
No sign change ⇒ point of inflection
traps: Don't give the x-value when the maximum value is asked
f′(c) = 0 does not always mean an extremum (x³ at 0)
A local max need not be larger than every local min

topics.t: Second derivative test and absolute extrema
topics.h: Sometimes checking signs on both sides is slow. The second derivative test decides max or min with one number.
p: Second derivative test: if f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0, c is a local maximum; if f″(c) > 0, a local minimum.
If f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) = 0, the test fails; go back to the first derivative test.
Absolute extrema on a closed interval [a, b]: evaluate f at every critical point in (a, b) and at the end points a and b. The largest is the absolute max, the smallest is the absolute min.
A continuous function on a closed interval always has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.
Tangents and normals and approximations are not in the current CBSE syllabus.

ex.q: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 36x + 1 on [1, 5].
ex.a: Absolute max 56 at x = 5; absolute min 24 at x = 1.

topics.rl: To find the highest and lowest temperature of a day between 6 am and 6 pm, you must check both the turning points of the temperature curve and the two end times, just like an absolute extremum on [a, b].

rv.summary: If f′(c) = 0, then f″(c) < 0 means local maximum and f″(c) > 0 means local minimum; f″(c) = 0 means the test fails. On [a, b], compare f at critical points and end points for absolute extrema.
focus: Use the second derivative test
Find absolute max and min on a closed interval
Handle cases where the test fails
remember: f″(c) < 0 ⇒ local max; f″(c) > 0 ⇒ local min
Absolute extrema: check critical points and both end points
A continuous function on [a, b] has an absolute max and min
traps: Don't forget the end points
f″(c) = 0 does not prove an inflection; use the first derivative test
Don't add max of sin and max of cos to get the max of sin x + cos x

topics.h: What size of square should you cut from the corners of a sheet to make the biggest open box? Calculus gives the exact answer, not a guess.
p: Method: name the variable, write the quantity to optimise as a function of ONE variable using the given condition, differentiate, find critical points, and confirm max/min with f″ or a sign check.
Two positive numbers with fixed sum S: product is largest when both are S/2.
Open box from a square sheet of side a, cutting squares of side x: V = x(a − 2x)², maximum at x = a/6.

Classic results: a rectangle of maximum area inscribed in a circle is a square; a closed cylinder of fixed volume has least surface when h = 2r; a cone of maximum volume in a sphere of radius R has height 4R/3.
Profit P = R − C is maximum where P′(x) = 0 and P″(x) < 0.

ex.q: A square tin sheet of side 18 cm has equal squares cut from each corner and the sides folded up. Find the cut size for the largest box.
st: Let the cut be x cm. V = x(18 − 2x)², 0 < x < 9.
ex.a: Cut 3 cm squares; maximum volume 432 cm³.

topics.rl: Can makers want to hold a given volume using the least metal. Calculus says the best closed can has h = 2r, that is, its height equals its diameter.

rv.summary: Write the quantity to optimise as a function of one variable, set its derivative to zero, and confirm with f″ or a sign check. Know the classic results for boxes, rectangles, cylinders and profit.
focus: Set up the function from the given condition
Find the optimum and confirm max or min
Answer the exact question: the value or the input
remember: Fixed sum S: product largest at S/2 each
Open box from square of side a: cut x = a/6
Rectangle in circle: square, area 2r²; closed can of fixed volume: h = 2r
Profit max where P′ = 0 and P″ < 0
traps: Don't report the output when the maximum profit is asked (or vice versa)
Reduce to ONE variable before differentiating
Check the domain, e.g. 0 < x < 9 for the box

topics.h: If speed is the derivative of distance, how do you get distance back from speed? Run differentiation in reverse: integrate.
p: Integration reverses differentiation and also measures areas. If F′(x) = f(x), F is an anti-derivative (primitive) of f and ∫f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where C is the constant of integration.
Standard results: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1), ∫(1/x) dx = log|x| + C, ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C, ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/log a + C.
Trig: ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C, ∫cos x dx = sin x + C, ∫sec²x dx = tan x + C, ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x + C, ∫sec x tan x dx = sec x + C, ∫cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x + C.
Inverse trig: ∫dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹x + C, ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x + C, ∫dx/(x√(x² − 1)) = sec⁻¹x + C.
Properties: ∫[f ± g] dx = ∫f dx ± ∫g dx, ∫kf dx = k∫f dx, and d/dx ∫f(x) dx = f(x). An initial condition fixes C.

ex.q: Find f(x) if f′(x) = 3x² + 2x and f(1) = 5.

topics.rl: From a train's speed log you can recover the distance it covered: integrate speed with respect to time.

rv.summary: Integration reverses differentiation: if F′ = f then ∫f dx = F + C. Learn the standard power, exponential, trigonometric and inverse trig integrals, and use an initial condition to find C.
focus: Integrate term by term using standard results
Simplify the integrand before integrating
Find C from a given value like f(1) = 5
remember: ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C; ∫sec²x dx = tan x + C; ∫sec x tan x dx = sec x + C
∫dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹x + C; ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x + C
traps: Divide by the new power, don't multiply
The power rule fails at n = −1
Don't forget the constant C (and to find it when a condition is given)

topics.h: ∫2x cos(x²) dx looks scary until you spot that 2x is the derivative of x². Substitution is the art of spotting that pair.
p: If the integrand contains g(x) and g′(x), put t = g(x), so dt = g′(x) dx, and integrate in t. Return to x at the end.
∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C.
∫tan x dx = log|sec x| + C, ∫cot x dx = log|sin x| + C.
∫sec x dx = log|sec x + tan x| + C, ∫cosec x dx = log|cosec x − cot x| + C.

ex.q: Find ∫(log x)²/x dx.
st: Put t = log x, so dt = (1/x) dx.
The integral becomes ∫t² dt = t³/3 + C.

topics.rl: Physicists simplify radioactive-decay integrals by substituting t = −λx, turning messy exponentials into ∫eᵗ dt.

rv.summary: If an integrand contains g(x) and g′(x), put t = g(x) and dt = g′(x) dx, integrate in t, and return to x. Key results: ∫f′/f dx = log|f| + C, and the integrals of tan, cot, sec and cosec.
focus: Spot the inner function and its derivative
Use the f′/f pattern
Handle linear substitutions like 3x + 5
remember: ∫tan x dx = log|sec x| + C; ∫cot x dx = log|sin x| + C
∫sec x dx = log|sec x + tan x| + C; ∫cosec x dx = log|cosec x − cot x| + C
traps: Divide by the coefficient of x in a linear substitution
Don't lose the minus sign when dt = −sin x dx
Keep the 1/2 when dt = 2x dx

topics.h: ∫sin²x dx has no direct formula. One identity, cos 2x = 1 − 2 sin²x, turns it into a two-second job.
p: Reduce powers: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2.
Cubes: sin³x = (3 sin x − sin 3x)/4, cos³x = (3 cos x + cos 3x)/4.
Products to sums: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B); 2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A − B); 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B).
tan²x = sec²x − 1 and cot²x = cosec²x − 1.
Odd powers can also be done by substitution, e.g. cos³x = (1 − sin²x) cos x with t = sin x.

ex.q: Find ∫sin 2x cos 3x dx.

topics.rl: Electrical engineers at power grids average sin²(ωt) over a cycle to compute the RMS value of AC mains (230 V in India); the identity sin² = (1 − cos 2θ)/2 is how.

rv.summary: Powers and products of sines and cosines are integrated after rewriting them with identities: half-angle formulas for squares, triple-angle formulas for cubes, and product-to-sum formulas for products.
focus: Integrate sin²x, cos²x, tan²x and sin³x
Convert products like sin 2x cos 3x to sums
Use substitution for odd powers
remember: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B); 2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A − B)
traps: Don't treat sin²x like x²
Keep the factor 1/2 from product-to-sum formulas
tan²x is sec²x − 1, not sec²x + 1

topics.h: Six formulas unlock a huge chunk of board questions. Learn their shapes and you will spot them instantly.
p: ∫dx/(x² − a²) = (1/2a) log|(x − a)/(x + a)| + C.
∫dx/(a² − x²) = (1/2a) log|(a + x)/(a − x)| + C.
∫dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C.
∫dx/√(x² − a²) = log|x + √(x² − a²)| + C and ∫dx/√(x² + a²) = log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C.
∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. If the coefficient of x² is not 1, factor it out first (e.g. 9x² + 4 = 9(x² + 4/9)).

ex.q: Find ∫dx/(9x² + 4).

topics.rl: Many formulas in physics and engineering, from orbits to electric circuits, reduce to these standard forms; engineers recognise them the same way you will.

rv.summary: Six standard forms handle x² ± a² and a² − x², with or without a square root. When the coefficient of x² is not 1, factor it out first.
focus: Match an integrand to the right standard form
Factor out the x² coefficient correctly
Combine with substitution, e.g. t = x³
remember: ∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫dx/√(x² ± a²) = log|x + √(x² ± a²)| + C
traps: Don't put 1/a in the sin⁻¹ form
Don't mix up the x² − a² and a² − x² forms
Use 1/(2a), not 1/a, in the log forms

topics.h: ∫dx/(x² − 6x + 13) does not match any formula, until you write x² − 6x + 13 = (x − 3)² + 4.
p: For ∫dx/(ax² + bx + c) or ∫dx/√(ax² + bx + c): complete the square, ax² + bx + c = a[(x + b/2a)² ± k²], then use a standard form.
For ∫(px + q)/(ax² + bx + c) dx: write px + q = A·d/dx(ax² + bx + c) + B = A(2ax + b) + B, and find A and B by comparing coefficients.
The A part gives A log|ax² + bx + c|; the B part is a completing-the-square integral.
For ∫(px + q)/√(ax² + bx + c) dx, the A part gives 2A√(ax² + bx + c).
Always factor out the coefficient of x² before completing the square.

ex.q: Find ∫dx/(x² − 6x + 13).

topics.rl: Engineers analysing how a spring or a car's suspension settles meet integrals of 1/(quadratic); completing the square is their first step too.

rv.summary: For a quadratic in the denominator (or under a root), complete the square and use a standard form. For a linear numerator, write it as A × (derivative of the quadratic) + B.
focus: Complete the square correctly
Find A and B by comparing coefficients
Use f′/f and 2√f results for the A part
remember: ∫(px + q)/(ax² + bx + c) dx: A part gives A log|ax² + bx + c|
traps: Factor out the coefficient of x² before completing the square
Watch the sign inside 5 − 4x − x² = 9 − (x + 2)²
Use sin⁻¹ only for a² − t² under a root

topics.h: 1/((x + 1)(x + 2)) splits into 1/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 2), and each piece is just a log. Breaking fractions apart is the trick.
p: P(x)/Q(x) is proper if deg P < deg Q. If improper, divide first to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction.
Distinct linear factors: (px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b).
Repeated factor: (px² + qx + r)/((x − a)²(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)² + C/(x − b).
Quadratic factor x² + bx + c that does not factor: (px² + qx + r)/((x − a)(x² + bx + c)) = A/(x − a) + (Bx + C)/(x² + bx + c).
Substitute first when needed: with t = sin x or t = eˣ, many trig or exponential integrals become rational functions of t.
topics.rl: In medicine, the amount of a drug in the blood is often modelled by simple exponential pieces, and partial fractions are one way of splitting a complicated model into those pieces.

rv.summary: A proper rational function is split into partial fractions, each of which integrates to a log or tan⁻¹ term. Improper fractions must be divided first.
focus: Choose the correct partial-fraction form
Find constants by substituting roots
Use t = sin x or t = x² to reduce to rational form
remember: Distinct linear: A/(x − a) + B/(x − b)
Repeated: A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)² + C/(x − b)
Improper (deg P ≥ deg Q): divide first
traps: Don't use a constant numerator over an irreducible quadratic
Don't split an improper fraction without dividing

topics.h: The product rule has a reverse twin. When an integral is a product like x cos x, integration by parts swaps a hard problem for an easy one.
p: ∫u·v dx = u∫v dx − ∫[u′ · ∫v dx] dx, where u is the first function and v the second.
Choose the first function by ILATE: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential (earlier in the list = first function).
For ∫log x dx or ∫sin⁻¹x dx, take 1 as the second function.
Results: ∫x cos x dx = x sin x + cos x + C; ∫x eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C; ∫log x dx = x log x − x + C.
For ∫eˣ sin x dx, apply parts twice; the original integral reappears, and you solve for it: ∫eˣ sin x dx = (eˣ/2)(sin x − cos x) + C.

ex.q: Find ∫x cos x dx.
st: ∫x cos x dx = x sin x − ∫1 · sin x dx.
ex.a: x sin x + cos x + C

topics.rl: Signal-processing engineers meet integrals like ∫t e^(−t) sin t dt when analysing radio and radar signals, and they apply integration by parts more than once.

rv.summary: Integration by parts: ∫u v dx = u∫v dx − ∫[u′ ∫v dx] dx, with u chosen by ILATE. Take 1 as v for log x or sin⁻¹x, and for eˣ sin x apply parts twice and solve for the integral.
focus: Choose u using ILATE
Evaluate ∫x eˣ, ∫log x, ∫x log x, ∫sin⁻¹x
Handle repeated parts and the cyclic case eˣ sin x
remember: ILATE: Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential
∫x eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C; ∫log x dx = x log x − x + C
∫eˣ sin x dx = (eˣ/2)(sin x − cos x) + C
traps: Don't choose eˣ as u when an algebraic factor is present
Watch the sign of the second term
Don't stop after one application when the power is 2 or more

topics.t: Special parts: eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] and √ forms
topics.h: Some integrals look terrible but collapse in one line, because they are secretly the derivative of eˣ f(x).
p: ∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] dx = eˣ f(x) + C, since d/dx[eˣ f(x)] = eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)].
Spot the pair: sin x and cos x, tan⁻¹x and 1/(1 + x²), 1/x and −1/x², x and 1.
∫√(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C.
∫√(x² + a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) + (a²/2) log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C.
∫√(x² − a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² − a²) − (a²/2) log|x + √(x² − a²)| + C. For quadratics under a root, complete the square first.

ex.q: Find ∫eˣ(tan⁻¹x + 1/(1 + x²)) dx.
st: Let f(x) = tan⁻¹x; then f′(x) = 1/(1 + x²).

topics.rl: Civil engineers find the area of a semicircular arch or gate using ∫√(a² − x²) dx, the formula you learn here.

rv.summary: If the integrand is eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)], the answer is eˣ f(x) + C. Three square-root formulas handle √(a² − x²), √(x² + a²) and √(x² − a²).
focus: Spot f and f′ in eˣ[f + f′]
Apply the three √ formulas with the right a²/2 term
remember: ∫√(x² + a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) + (a²/2) log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C
∫√(x² − a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² − a²) − (a²/2) log|x + √(x² − a²)| + C
traps: Pick f so that the other term is exactly f′
Use a²/2, not a²
The log term is + for x² + a² and − for x² − a²

topics.t: Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem
topics.h: How much rain fell over a day if you know the rate every hour? Add up rate × time: that is a definite integral, and one theorem makes it easy.
p: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the area under y = f(x) between x = a and x = b, above the x-axis, when f ≥ 0. a and b are the lower and upper limits.
Area function: A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt.
First fundamental theorem: A′(x) = f(x) for continuous f.
Second fundamental theorem: if F′ = f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). The constant C cancels, so ignore it.
Definite integral as the limit of a sum is not in the current CBSE syllabus.

ex.q: Evaluate ∫₁² x³ dx.

topics.rl: If a rain gauge records the rainfall rate (mm per hour) through the day, the total rainfall for the day is the definite integral of that rate over time.

rv.summary: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) where F is any anti-derivative, so C cancels. The area function A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt has A′(x) = f(x).
focus: Evaluate definite integrals with the second fundamental theorem
Differentiate an area function
Use standard anti-derivatives at the limits
traps: Subtract in the order F(b) − F(a)
Don't use +cos x as the anti-derivative of sin x
Don't integrate again when F′(x) is asked

topics.h: When you substitute in a definite integral, change the limits too. Then you never have to switch back to x.
p: Put t = g(x), dt = g′(x) dx, and change the limits: x = a gives t = g(a), x = b gives t = g(b).
Then ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = ∫ from g(a) to g(b) of f(t) dt.
Do not mix: either change limits and stay in t, or go back to x and use the old limits.
∫₀¹ 2x/(1 + x²) dx = log 2 (t = 1 + x², t from 1 to 2).
∫₀¹ tan⁻¹x/(1 + x²) dx = π²/32 (t = tan⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/4).

ex.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin x cos x dx.
st: Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx.

topics.rl: Railway engineers converting a curved track's length integral into a simpler one change the variable and limits together, exactly as here.

rv.summary: In a definite integral, substitute t = g(x) and change the limits to g(a) and g(b); then finish in t without returning to x.
focus: Choose t and find dt
Convert both limits correctly
Evaluate the t-integral
remember: ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = ∫ from g(a) to g(b) of f(t) dt
traps: Don't keep the old x-limits after substituting
Don't forget factors like 1/2 from dt = 2x dx
Don't mix x-limits with a t-integral

topics.t: Properties of definite integrals I and modulus integrals
topics.h: Some definite integrals that look impossible fall in two lines, not by integrating harder but by using a property cleverly.
p: P0: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt (the variable is a dummy).
P1: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = −∫ from b to a of f(x) dx; in particular ∫ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0.
P2: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᶜ f(x) dx + ∫ from c to b of f(x) dx for any c.
P3: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx. Adding the two versions often cancels the hard part.
Modulus: split at the zeros of the expression inside |…| and integrate each piece with the correct sign.

ex.q: Evaluate ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of dx/(1 + √(tan x)).
st: Write tan x = sin x/cos x: I = ∫√cos x/(√cos x + √sin x) dx.
P3 (a + b = π/2) turns cos ↔ sin: I = ∫√sin x/(√sin x + √cos x) dx.
Add: 2I = ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of 1 dx = π/6.

topics.rl: A scooter goes forward and then comes back. To find the total distance (not the net displacement), you split the velocity integral where the velocity changes sign, just like a modulus integral.

rv.summary: Definite integrals can be split at any point, change sign when the limits are swapped, and satisfy ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx. Modulus integrals are split at the zeros inside the modulus.
focus: Evaluate modulus integrals by splitting
Use P2 to find a missing piece
Use P3 and add to cancel the hard part
remember: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx
traps: Don't integrate |f| without splitting at its zeros
Halve after adding I to itself
Swapping limits changes the sign

topics.t: Properties II: even, odd and classic results
topics.h: ∫ from −1 to 1 of sin⁵x cos⁴x dx: no integration needed. The answer is 0, and symmetry tells you why.
p: P4: ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx.
P5: ∫₀^(2a) f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx if f(2a − x) = f(x), and = 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x).
P6: ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx if f is even (f(−x) = f(x)), and = 0 if f is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)).
Classic: ∫₀^(π/2) sinⁿx/(sinⁿx + cosⁿx) dx = π/4 for every n; ∫₀^(π/2) log sin x dx = −(π/2) log 2.
Strategy for any integral: simplify, try substitution, partial fractions, parts, then properties.

ex.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin x)/(√(sin x) + √(cos x)) dx.
st: Call it I. By P4, replacing x with π/2 − x: I = ∫₀^(π/2) √(cos x)/(√(cos x) + √(sin x)) dx.

topics.rl: Physicists use symmetry all the time: an odd function integrates to zero over symmetric limits, so whole parts of a long calculation cancel instantly.

rv.summary: ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx; over [−a, a], even functions give twice the half-integral and odd functions give 0. Classic results include π/4 for sinⁿ/(sinⁿ + cosⁿ) and −(π/2) log 2.
focus: Use odd/even symmetry
Apply P4 and add the two forms
Use P5 for intervals like [0, 2π]
traps: Not every integral over symmetric limits is 0; only odd functions
Don't forget to halve after adding
log sin x ≤ 0 on (0, π/2), so its integral is negative

topics.t: Area under a curve: vertical and horizontal strips
topics.h: Slice a region into thin strips, add their areas, and shrink the strips to zero width. That sum becomes a definite integral.
p: Definite integrals give areas of regions bounded by curves, lines and the axes.
Vertical strips: the area between y = f(x) ≥ 0, the x-axis and the lines x = a, x = b is ∫ₐᵇ y dx.
Horizontal strips: the area between x = g(y) ≥ 0, the y-axis and y = c, y = d is ∫ from c to d of x dy.
A straight line region is a trapezium or triangle, so you can check the integral with geometry.
Always sketch first: it tells you which strips to use and where the limits are.

ex.q: Find the area bounded by y = x², the x-axis and the lines x = 1 and x = 2.
st: The curve lies above the x-axis on [1, 2].

topics.rl: Surveyors estimate the area of a plot with a curved boundary by measuring its width at regular intervals and adding thin strips, which is integration in practice.

rv.summary: The area between y = f(x) ≥ 0, the x-axis and x = a, x = b is ∫ₐᵇ y dx; with horizontal strips, the area next to the y-axis is ∫ x dy. Sketch first to pick strips and limits.
focus: Find areas under curves like x², x³, √x, eˣ
Use horizontal strips for curves x = g(y)
Check line regions with geometry
remember: Horizontal strips: Area = ∫ from c to d of x dy
traps: Don't mix up dx and dy strips
Subtract the lower-limit value, e.g. e⁰ = 1
Use the right power: ∫√x dx = (2/3)x^(3/2)

topics.t: Regions below the axis and on both sides
topics.h: ∫₀^(2π) sin x dx = 0, yet the curve clearly encloses area with the axis. Integrals can cancel; areas never do.
p: If f(x) ≤ 0 on [a, b], the region lies below the x-axis and its area is |∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx|.
If the curve crosses the axis at c, split: Area = |∫ₐᶜ f dx| + |∫ from c to b of f dx|.
y = sin x on [0, 2π] gives area 2 + 2 = 4, though the integral is 0. Similarly y = cos x on [0, 2π] gives area 4.
y = x³ on [−2, 1] gives area 4 + 1/4 = 17/4.
Modulus curves like y = |x + 3| lie above the axis: integrate piece by piece.

ex.q: Find the area bounded by y = cos x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2π.
st: Pieces: ∫₀^(π/2) cos x = 1, |∫ from π/2 to 3π/2 of cos x| = 2, ∫ from 3π/2 to 2π of cos x = 1.

topics.rl: A bank account's net change over a month can be zero even when lots of money went in and out. The total money moved adds the absolute amounts, just as area adds the pieces above and below the axis as positives.

rv.summary: Parts of a region below the x-axis give negative integrals, so take absolute values and split the region where the curve crosses the axis. The area can be positive even when the integral is 0.
focus: Split at the points where the curve crosses the x-axis
Find areas for sin x, cos x, x³ and lines on both sides
Handle modulus curves piece by piece
remember: Area below the axis = |∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx|
y = sin x on [0, 2π]: area 4, integral 0
traps: Don't report a negative or zero integral as the area
Don't integrate across a crossing point without splitting
Area is always positive

topics.t: Area of a circle and an ellipse
topics.h: You have used πr² since Class 7. Now prove it with calculus, and get the ellipse's area πab for free.
p: Circle x² + y² = a²: by symmetry, area = 4 × (first-quadrant area) = 4∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx.
Using ∫√(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a), the first quadrant gives (a²/2)(π/2) = πa²/4, so the area is πa².
Ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: y = (b/a)√(a² − x²) in the first quadrant, so area = 4(b/a)∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx = πab.
A circle is the ellipse with a = b.
Use symmetry about both axes to integrate over one quadrant only.

ex.q: Find the area enclosed by the ellipse x²/16 + y²/9 = 1.

topics.rl: Planetary orbits are ellipses. ISRO's Mangalyaan orbit around Mars was elliptical, and Kepler's second law links area swept by an orbit to time, so these area formulas matter in mission planning.

rv.summary: Using symmetry and the formula for ∫√(a² − x²) dx, the circle x² + y² = a² has area πa² and the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 has area πab.
focus: Find areas of circles and ellipses (whole or a quarter)
Rewrite equations like 4x² + 9y² = 36 in standard form
Set up the first-quadrant integral
traps: Use a and b, not a² and b²
Divide to get 1 on the right side before reading a and b
Don't confuse area πa² with circumference 2πa

topics.h: A satellite dish has a parabolic cross-section. How much area does the parabola enclose up to a given line? Two neat formulas answer it.
p: For y² = 4ax and x = k: the region is symmetric about the x-axis, so area = 2∫₀ᵏ 2√(ax) dx = (8/3)√a · k^(3/2).
For x² = 4ay and y = k: area = 2∫₀ᵏ 2√(ay) dy.
First-quadrant regions: use only y ≥ 0, x ≥ 0 and the given lines as limits.
Choose strips wisely: for x² = 4y and the y-axis, horizontal strips (∫ x dy) are often easier.
Area between two curves and between a curve and a slanting line are not in the current CBSE syllabus.

ex.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 9x, x = 2, x = 4 and the x-axis in the first quadrant.

topics.rl: Parabolic solar cookers concentrate sunlight at the focus; the cross-section of the reflector is a parabola, and its area is found with integrals like these.

rv.summary: For a parabola and a line, use symmetry about the parabola's axis and choose the easier strips. In the first quadrant take only the positive branch, e.g. y = 2√x or x = 2√y.
focus: Area of y² = 4ax with x = k, and x² = 4ay with y = k
First-quadrant regions with horizontal strips
Use the right branch and limits
remember: Double the upper half for a region symmetric about the x-axis
traps: Don't forget the half below the x-axis when the region is symmetric
In the first quadrant, don't count both sides of the y-axis
Keep the coefficient, e.g. y = 3√x from y² = 9x

topics.t: Order and degree of a differential equation
topics.h: Population growth, cooling chai, a swinging pendulum: each is described by an equation that involves a rate of change, a differential equation.
p: Differential equations model growth, decay, motion and many other changing quantities.

A differential equation involves derivatives of a dependent variable (y) with respect to an independent variable (x). If there is only one independent variable, it is an ordinary differential equation.
Order: the order of the highest derivative present.
Degree: when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives, the power of the highest-order derivative (after clearing radicals and fractions in the derivatives).
Degree is not defined if a derivative appears inside a function like sin(y′), e^(y″) or log(y′). Order and degree (when defined) are always positive integers.

ex.q: Find the order and degree of (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0.
st: The highest derivative is d²y/dx², so the order is 2.
The equation is a polynomial in the derivatives.
The power of d²y/dx² is 3, so the degree is 3.

topics.rl: Newton's law of cooling, which describes how a cup of hot chai cools, dT/dt = −k(T − Tₛ), is a first-order, first-degree differential equation.

rv.summary: The order of a differential equation is the order of its highest derivative. The degree is the power of that derivative, defined only when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives.
focus: Find order and degree of a given equation
Clear radicals before reading the degree
Spot equations whose degree is not defined
remember: Degree = power of the highest-order derivative (polynomial form only)
Degree not defined if a derivative is inside sin, e^, log etc.
traps: Don't use the highest power anywhere as the degree
Order is about which derivative, degree is about its power
Square away a radical before finding the degree

topics.h: y = A cos x + B sin x solves y″ + y = 0 for every A and B. A whole family of curves, one equation. Pick A and B, and you get one particular member.
p: A solution of a differential equation is a function that satisfies it.
General solution: contains arbitrary constants. Particular solution: obtained by giving the constants definite values (no arbitrary constants left).
The number of arbitrary constants in the general solution equals the order of the equation.
