To verify a solution: differentiate the given function as many times as needed, substitute into the equation, and check both sides match.
Forming a differential equation from a given general solution (eliminating constants) is not in the current CBSE syllabus.

ex.q: Verify that y = eˣ + 1 is a solution of y″ − y′ = 0.
ex.a: Yes, y = eˣ + 1 satisfies y″ − y′ = 0.

topics.rl: The equation of motion of a thrown cricket ball has a general solution that covers every possible throw; the release point and speed (the initial conditions) pick out one particular path.

rv.summary: A general solution has as many arbitrary constants as the order, while a particular solution has none. To verify a solution, differentiate it and substitute into the equation.
focus: Count constants in general and particular solutions
Verify that a function satisfies an equation
Find a particular solution from a given point
remember: Number of arbitrary constants in general solution = order
traps: Don't confuse order with degree when counting constants
Don't take the y-value as C directly; substitute properly
y″ + y = 0 needs y″ = −y, not y″ = y

topics.h: If dy/dx = g(x)h(y), you can put every y on one side and every x on the other, then integrate both. It is the first method every board paper tests.
p: Form: dy/dx = F(x, y) = g(x) h(y).
Separate: dy/h(y) = g(x) dx (with h(y) ≠ 0).
Integrate both sides: ∫dy/h(y) = ∫g(x) dx + C. That is the general solution.
For a particular solution, substitute the initial condition to find C.
Common results: dy/dx = ky gives y = Ae^(kx); dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²) gives tan⁻¹ y = tan⁻¹ x + C.

ex.q: Find the particular solution of dy/dx = −4xy², given y = 1 when x = 0.

topics.rl: Drug half-life calculations start from dC/dt = −kC, a variable separable equation whose solution is exponential decay.

rv.summary: If dy/dx = g(x)h(y), separate as dy/h(y) = g(x) dx and integrate both sides. Use an initial condition to find C for a particular solution.
focus: Recognise separable equations (factorise if needed)
Integrate both sides correctly
Find particular solutions
remember: dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²) ⇒ tan⁻¹ y = tan⁻¹ x + C
traps: Don't lose the minus sign in ∫e⁻ʸ dy = −e⁻ʸ
x + y is not separable; try factorising expressions like 1 + x + y + xy
Don't forget the constant A in y = Ae^(kx)

topics.h: Money, microbes and mountains: compound interest, bacterial growth and the shape of a curve all fall to the same separate-and-integrate idea.
p: 'Rate proportional to amount' means dN/dt = kN, which gives N = N₀ e^(kt): growth if k > 0, decay if k < 0.
Continuous compounding at r% per year: dP/dt = (r/100)P, so P = P₀ e^(rt/100).
If a quantity grows by a fixed factor in a fixed time, use that to find k, e.g. doubling: e^(kT) = 2 ⇒ k = (log 2)/T.
A curve whose slope at (x, y) is given: write dy/dx = (given expression), solve, and use the given point to find C.
Always state what each variable means and include units in the final answer.

ex.q: Find the curve through (−2, 3) whose slope at (x, y) is 2x/y².

topics.rl: A fixed deposit with continuous compounding would grow by dP/dt = (r/100)P. Banks usually compound fixed deposits quarterly, but the continuous model is a close and simple estimate.

rv.summary: 'Rate proportional to amount' gives dN/dt = kN and N = N₀e^(kt): growth for k > 0 and decay for k < 0. Continuous interest follows P = P₀e^(rt/100), and slope problems give dy/dx directly.
focus: Model growth, decay and continuous interest
Find k from a doubling time
Find a curve from its slope and a point
traps: Convert r% to r/100
n doublings multiply by 2ⁿ, not 2n
Exponential decay is not a straight-line fall

topics.h: dy/dx = (x + y)/x does not separate. But substitute y = vx and suddenly it does. That trick is the whole method.
p: F(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n if F(λx, λy) = λⁿ F(x, y) for all λ ≠ 0.
dy/dx = F(x, y) is homogeneous if F is homogeneous of degree 0, i.e. F(x, y) = g(y/x).
Method: put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. The equation becomes separable in v and x.
If dx/dy = G(x, y) with G of degree 0, put x = vy instead.
After integrating, replace v by y/x, then use any initial condition to find C.

ex.q: Solve dy/dx = (x + y)/x.
st: Degree 0: (λx + λy)/(λx) = (x + y)/x. Put y = vx.
v + x dv/dx = 1 + v ⇒ x dv/dx = 1 ⇒ dv = dx/x.
v = log|x| + C ⇒ y/x = log|x| + C.

topics.rl: Homogeneous equations appear whenever a rate depends only on the direction y/x and not on the distance from the origin, for example in some curve-tracing and flow problems.

rv.summary: dy/dx = F(x, y) is homogeneous when F is a function of y/x alone (degree 0). Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, and the equation becomes separable.
focus: Find the degree of a homogeneous function
Check if an equation is homogeneous
Solve with y = vx (or x = vy)
remember: F(λx, λy) = λⁿF(x, y): degree n
y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x dv/dx
For dx/dy = G(x/y), put x = vy
traps: Don't forget the product rule in d(vx)/dx
Mixed-degree terms or constants make it non-homogeneous
Replace v by y/x at the end

topics.h: dy/dx + Py = Q: one magic multiplier, the integrating factor, turns the left side into the derivative of a single product.
p: Linear form: dy/dx + Py = Q, where P and Q are functions of x only (or constants).
Integrating factor IF = e^(∫P dx).
Solution: y · IF = ∫(Q · IF) dx + C.
If the equation is linear in x: dx/dy + P₁x = Q₁ (P₁, Q₁ functions of y), then IF = e^(∫P₁ dy) and x · IF = ∫(Q₁ · IF) dy + C.
Always rewrite into standard form first (divide by the coefficient of dy/dx).

ex.q: Solve x dy/dx + 2y = x² (x ≠ 0).
st: Standard form: dy/dx + (2/x)y = x. So P = 2/x, Q = x.
IF = e^(∫2/x dx) = e^(2 log x) = x².
y · x² = ∫x · x² dx = x⁴/4 + C.

topics.rl: In electrical circuits, an inductor–resistor (RL) circuit obeys L di/dt + Ri = E, a linear equation solved with the same integrating factor.

rv.summary: A linear equation dy/dx + Py = Q is solved with IF = e^(∫P dx), giving y · IF = ∫Q · IF dx + C. If it is linear in x, use dx/dy + P₁x = Q₁ instead.
focus: Write the equation in standard form
Find the integrating factor
Solve and apply initial conditions
remember: Linear in x: x · IF = ∫(Q₁ · IF) dy + C, IF = e^(∫P₁ dy)
traps: Divide by the coefficient of dy/dx before reading P
Divide C by the IF too
Use Q, not P, inside the integral, and P, not Q, in the IF

topics.t: Curves from slopes and choosing the method
topics.h: In the exam, the hardest step is often deciding which method to use. A quick checklist turns panic into a plan.
p: Checklist: Can it be written as g(x) h(y)? Use separation. Is it a function of y/x only? Use y = vx. Is it dy/dx + Py = Q? Use the integrating factor.
Slope problems: 'slope at (x, y) is …' means dy/dx = … . Solve, then use the given point.
Example: the curve through the origin with slope x + y at (x, y) satisfies dy/dx − y = x.
Some equations fit more than one type; choose the easiest.
Always verify the final answer by substituting back if time allows.

ex.q: Find the curve through the origin whose slope at every point (x, y) is x + y.
st: dy/dx = x + y ⇒ dy/dx − y = x (linear, P = −1, Q = x).

topics.rl: Weather forecasting models solve many differential equations together; recognising the type of each piece and picking the right method is a key skill there too.

rv.summary: Choose the method by the form: separable if it splits as g(x)h(y), homogeneous if it depends only on y/x, linear if it is dy/dx + Py = Q. Slope problems mean dy/dx equals the given expression.
focus: Pick the right method for an equation
Solve curve problems with a given point
Recognise when an equation is not linear
remember: Separable: g(x)h(y); homogeneous: g(y/x); linear: dy/dx + Py = Q
'Slope at (x, y) is f' means dy/dx = f
traps: dy/dx − y/x = x² is linear, not homogeneous
Terms like y² make an equation non-linear
Don't forget the constant before using the given point

topics.t: Vectors, position vectors and direction cosines
topics.h: 'Go 5 km' is useless to a pilot. 'Go 5 km north-east' is an instruction. That difference between a scalar and a vector is where this chapter begins.
p: Scalars have magnitude only (mass, time, speed, temperature). Vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force).
A vector is a directed line segment AB with initial point A and terminal point B; its magnitude is the length |AB|.
Position vector of P(x, y, z): OP = xi + yj + zk, with |OP| = √(x² + y² + z²).
If OP makes angles α, β, γ with the x-, y-, z-axes, then l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ are its direction cosines, and l² + m² + n² = 1.
Direction ratios are any numbers a, b, c proportional to l, m, n; for r = ai + bj + ck, l = a/|r|, m = b/|r|, n = c/|r|.

ex.q: Find the direction cosines of the vector i + 2j + 2k.

topics.rl: Air traffic controllers at Delhi airport give each plane a velocity vector: speed plus heading. Two planes with the same speed but different headings are on very different paths.

rv.summary: A vector has magnitude and direction; the position vector of P(x, y, z) is xi + yj + zk with length √(x² + y² + z²). Its direction cosines l, m, n satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1.
focus: Find magnitude and direction cosines of a vector
Use l² + m² + n² = 1 to find a missing angle
Tell direction ratios from direction cosines
traps: Divide components by |r| to get direction cosines
Direction ratios need not satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1
Square the cosines: cos²60° = 1/4

topics.h: Two cricket fielders running in the same direction at the same speed from different spots have equal velocity vectors, even though they start in different places.
p: Zero (null) vector 0: magnitude zero, initial and terminal points coincide; its direction is not defined (any direction).
Unit vector: magnitude 1; the unit vector along a is â. Coinitial vectors share the same initial point.
Collinear (parallel) vectors lie along the same or parallel lines, whatever their magnitudes or senses.
Equal vectors: same magnitude and same direction, regardless of initial points. Negative of AB is BA, with the same magnitude and opposite direction.
Free vectors can be moved parallel to themselves without change; in this chapter all vectors are free vectors.

ex.q: In a square ABCD, classify AB and DC, and AB and CD.
st: AB and DC have the same length and point the same way, so they are equal vectors.
CD points opposite to AB with the same length, so CD = −AB.
All of them are collinear (parallel) vectors.

topics.rl: A map app's route is a chain of displacement vectors; sliding one leg of the route parallel to itself does not change that vector, because displacement vectors are free vectors.

rv.summary: Vectors may be zero, unit, coinitial, collinear, equal or negative of each other. Equal vectors need the same magnitude and the same direction; position does not matter for free vectors.
focus: Classify pairs of vectors in figures like parallelograms
Identify unit and zero vectors
Use perpendicular legs to find a displacement
remember: Equal vectors: same magnitude and direction
Collinear: along the same or parallel lines (any sense)
traps: Same magnitude alone does not make vectors equal
CD is not DC: CD = −DC
Opposite direction still counts as collinear

topics.h: A boat crossing the Ganga while the river pushes it downstream ends up somewhere neither push alone would take it. Vector addition finds where.
p: Triangle law: if a and b are two sides of a triangle in order (head to tail), the third side taken from the start to the end is a + b: AB + BC = AC.
So AB + BC + CA = 0 for any triangle ABC.
Parallelogram law: if a and b are adjacent sides from a common point, the diagonal from that point is a + b.
Properties: a + b = b + a (commutative), (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) (associative), a + 0 = a, a + (−a) = 0.
Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|, with equality only when a and b point the same way.

ex.q: In triangle ABC, simplify AB + BC + CA.
st: By the triangle law, AB + BC = AC.

topics.rl: Pilots flying from Mumbai to Chennai add the plane's air velocity to the wind velocity; the resultant vector is the actual ground track.

rv.summary: Vectors add head to tail (triangle law) or along the diagonal of a parallelogram. Addition is commutative and associative, and |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.
focus: Simplify sums like AB + BC + CA
Use the parallelogram law
Find the largest and smallest possible |a + b|
remember: AB + BC = AC; AB + BC + CA = 0
traps: Don't add magnitudes when adding vectors
Least |a + b| is ||a| − |b||, not always 0
Keep the minus sign in CA = −(a + b)

topics.h: Every vector in space is just a mix of three building blocks: i, j and k. Know the mix, and you know everything about the vector.
p: λa has magnitude |λ||a|; it points along a if λ > 0 and opposite if λ < 0. The unit vector along a is â = a/|a|.
r = xi + yj + zk: x, y, z are scalar components and xi, yj, zk are vector components.
Operations are componentwise; a = b exactly when corresponding components are equal.
a and b are collinear ⇔ b = λa for some scalar λ ⇔ their components are proportional.
Vector joining P(x₁, y₁, z₁) to Q(x₂, y₂, z₂): PQ = (x₂ − x₁)i + (y₂ − y₁)j + (z₂ − z₁)k.

ex.q: Find a vector of magnitude 14 in the direction of 2i − 3j + 6k.

topics.rl: A delivery drone's flight can be described leg by leg with components east, north and up; adding the components gives the drone's net position.

rv.summary: λa scales the length by |λ| and reverses direction when λ < 0. Vectors are added, compared and scaled componentwise, and two vectors are collinear exactly when their components are proportional.
focus: Find a unit vector and a vector of given magnitude
Find PQ from two points
Test collinearity by proportional components
traps: Subtract P from Q for PQ, not Q from P
Scalar components are numbers; vector components include i, j, k
Multiply the unit vector, not the vector, by the required magnitude

topics.h: Where exactly is the point two-thirds of the way from Pune to Mumbai on a straight road? The section formula answers instantly in vector form.
p: If P and Q have position vectors a and b, the point R dividing PQ internally in the ratio m : n has position vector (mb + na)/(m + n).
Externally in the ratio m : n (m ≠ n): (mb − na)/(m − n).
Mid-point of PQ: (a + b)/2 (internal division with m = n = 1).
Centroid of a triangle with vertices a, b, c: (a + b + c)/3.
Remember the 'cross' pattern: m goes with b (the far end), n with a (the near end).

ex.q: OP = i + 2j − k and OQ = −i + j + k. Find the point R dividing PQ internally in the ratio 2 : 1.

topics.rl: To place a station two-thirds of the way along a straight stretch of track between two points, a planner can use exactly this section formula.

rv.summary: The point dividing PQ internally in m : n is (mb + na)/(m + n), and externally (mb − na)/(m − n). The mid-point is (a + b)/2 and the centroid is (a + b + c)/3.
focus: Apply internal and external section formulas
Find mid-points and centroids
Pair m with the far end b
traps: Don't pair m with a
Use m − n, not m + n, for external division
Centroid uses 1/3, not 1/2

topics.h: Pull a cart with a rope at an angle and only part of your force moves it forward. The dot product measures exactly that useful part.
p: a · b = |a||b| cos θ, where θ (0 ≤ θ ≤ π) is the angle between a and b. The result is a scalar.
Properties: a · b = b · a, a · (b + c) = a · b + a · c, (λa) · b = λ(a · b).
i · i = j · j = k · k = 1 and i · j = j · k = k · i = 0. So (a₁i + a₂j + a₃k) · (b₁i + b₂j + b₃k) = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.
Angle: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).
a ⊥ b ⇔ a · b = 0 (for non-zero vectors). a · a = |a|².

ex.q: Find the angle between a = i + j and b = j + k.

topics.rl: In physics, work = F · d. A porter at a railway station carrying luggage horizontally does no work against gravity, since force and displacement are perpendicular.

rv.summary: a · b = |a||b| cos θ is a scalar, and in components it is a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃. Non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when a · b = 0.
focus: Compute dot products in components
Find the angle between two vectors
Find an unknown that makes vectors perpendicular
remember: a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃
i · i = 1, i · j = 0; a · a = |a|²
traps: (−2)(−2) = +4: watch signs
A zero dot product means perpendicular, not parallel
The dot product is a number, not a vector

topics.h: A wind of 20 km/h blows at an angle to a runway. How much of it is a headwind? That is the projection of the wind vector on the runway.
p: Projection of a on b = (a · b)/|b| = a · b̂. Its vector form is ((a · b)/|b|²) b.
The projection is positive if the angle is acute and negative if obtuse.
|a + b|² = |a|² + 2a · b + |b|², |a − b|² = |a|² − 2a · b + |b|², and (a + b) · (a − b) = |a|² − |b|².
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: |a · b| ≤ |a||b|. Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.
If |a + b| = |a − b|, then a · b = 0, so a ⊥ b.

ex.q: Find the projection of a = 2i + 3j + 2k on b = i + 2j + k.

topics.rl: Cricket analysts break a ball's velocity into a part along the pitch and a part across it; the along-pitch part is a projection.

rv.summary: The projection of a on b is (a · b)/|b|. Expansions like |a ± b|² = |a|² ± 2a · b + |b|² and (a + b) · (a − b) = |a|² − |b|² solve many magnitude problems.
focus: Find the projection of one vector on another
Use dot product identities to find magnitudes
Handle a + b + c = 0 type problems
remember: Projection of a on b = (a · b)/|b|
traps: Divide by |b| (the vector projected on), not |a|
Take the square root at the end when |x| is asked
Don't forget cross terms when expanding

topics.h: Tighten a bolt with a spanner: the turning effect points along the bolt, perpendicular to both the spanner and your push. That direction is a cross product.
p: a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂, where n̂ is the unit vector perpendicular to both, chosen by the right-hand rule. The result is a vector.
Anti-commutative: a × b = −(b × a). Distributive: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c. a × a = 0.
i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j; and j × i = −k, k × j = −i, i × k = −j; i × i = j × j = k × k = 0.
Component form: a × b = |i j k; a₁ a₂ a₃; b₁ b₂ b₃| (a 3 × 3 determinant).
Non-zero a and b are parallel ⇔ a × b = 0. (The scalar triple product is not in the current CBSE syllabus.)

ex.q: Find (i − 7j + 7k) × (3i − 2j + 2k).

topics.rl: Torque τ = r × F decides how a wind turbine in Tamil Nadu's Muppandal wind farm spins: only the force component perpendicular to the blade turns it.

rv.summary: a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂ is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, found by a 3 × 3 determinant. It is anti-commutative, and non-zero vectors are parallel exactly when a × b = 0.
focus: Compute a × b by the determinant
Use |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ
Find unknowns from a × b = 0
remember: i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j; reversed order gives the negative
traps: Don't forget the minus on the j term of the determinant
Use sin θ, not cos θ, for |a × b|
k × j = −i, not i

topics.t: Using the cross product: perpendicular vectors and areas
topics.h: Need the area of a triangular plot from three GPS points in 3D? One cross product and a half do it.
p: A unit vector perpendicular to both a and b: ±(a × b)/|a × b|.
Area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b: |a × b|.
Area of a triangle with sides a and b from one vertex: (1/2)|a × b|.
For a parallelogram given by its diagonals d₁ and d₂, area = (1/2)|d₁ × d₂|.
To find a vector satisfying given conditions, write it as xi + yj + zk and use the dot or cross product conditions to form equations.

ex.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, 1, 2), B(2, 3, 5), C(1, 5, 5).

topics.rl: The direction a flat solar panel faces is its normal, which can be found as the cross product of two of its edges; tilting the panel so this normal points towards the sun gives the most power.

rv.summary: (a × b)/|a × b| is a unit vector perpendicular to both a and b. |a × b| is the area of the parallelogram on a and b, and half of it is the area of the triangle.
focus: Find unit vectors perpendicular to two vectors
Find areas of parallelograms and triangles
Use diagonals to find a parallelogram's area
traps: Halve for a triangle, not for a parallelogram on its sides
Halve when the diagonals are given
Divide by the magnitude to get a unit vector

topics.t: Direction cosines and direction ratios of a line
topics.h: A drone climbs from a rooftop in Bengaluru towards a tower. Three numbers, its direction cosines, pin down that heading in 3D space.
p: Vector algebra lets us describe lines in space neatly. If a line makes angles α, β, γ with the x-, y-, z-axes, its direction cosines are l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ.
Direction ratios a, b, c are any numbers proportional to l, m, n. A line has infinitely many sets of direction ratios.
From direction ratios: l = a/√(a² + b² + c²), m = b/√(…), n = c/√(…) (or all with the opposite sign).
Line through P(x₁, y₁, z₁) and Q(x₂, y₂, z₂): direction ratios x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁; divide by PQ for direction cosines.
Three points are collinear if the direction ratios of AB and BC are proportional. (The derivation of l² + m² + n² = 1 is not in the current syllabus; the result is used.)

ex.q: Find the direction cosines of the line through P(−2, 4, −5) and Q(1, 2, 3).

topics.rl: If GPS gives the coordinates of a base camp and of a ledge above it, the differences of the coordinates are direction ratios of the straight rope line between them; any proportional set describes the same line.

rv.summary: A line's direction cosines are the cosines of its angles with the axes, and direction ratios are any numbers proportional to them. For the line through two points, the direction ratios are the coordinate differences.
focus: Convert direction ratios to direction cosines
Find direction ratios of the line through two points
Test three points for collinearity
remember: l = a/√(a² + b² + c²), and similarly m, n
Through P, Q: DRs x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁
traps: Divide by √(a² + b² + c²), not by a² + b² + c²
cos 135° is negative
A negative multiple of the DRs is still the same line

topics.t: Equation of a line in space
topics.h: One point and one direction: that is all you need to describe a straight line in space, whether it is a laser beam or a metro tunnel.
p: Vector form: a line through the point with position vector a, parallel to b, is r = a + λb (λ a real parameter).
Cartesian form: through (x₁, y₁, z₁) with direction ratios a, b, c: (x − x₁)/a = (y − y₁)/b = (z − z₁)/c.
To convert Cartesian to vector: read the point (x₁, y₁, z₁) and the direction (a, b, c) from the denominators.
A line parallel to a given line has the same direction ratios.
Watch signs: (x + 3)/2 means x₁ = −3. Write the form as x − x₁ before reading off the point.

ex.q: Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the line through (5, 2, −4) parallel to 3i + 2j − 8k.

topics.rl: A laser beam, or the centre line of a straight tunnel, is fixed by one starting point and one direction; every point on it fits r = a + λb.

rv.summary: A line through point a parallel to b is r = a + λb, or in Cartesian form (x − x₁)/a = (y − y₁)/b = (z − z₁)/c. The denominators give the direction.
focus: Write vector and Cartesian equations of a line
Read the point and direction from a given equation
Find lines through two points or parallel to a line
remember: Parallel lines have proportional direction ratios
traps: Rewrite (x + 3) as x − (−3) before reading the point
Don't swap the point and the direction
A zero denominator means that coordinate stays fixed

topics.h: Two runways at an airport cross at an angle. Find it from their direction vectors, with no protractor needed.
p: If lines have direction ratios a₁, b₁, c₁ and a₂, b₂, c₂, the acute angle θ between them satisfies cos θ = |a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂| / (√(a₁² + b₁² + c₁²) √(a₂² + b₂² + c₂²)).
In vector form: cos θ = |b₁ · b₂| / (|b₁||b₂|).
Perpendicular lines: a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0.
Parallel lines: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂.
With direction cosines, cos θ = |l₁l₂ + m₁m₂ + n₁n₂|.

ex.q: Find the angle between r = 3i + 2j − 4k + λ(i + 2j + 2k) and r = 5i − 2j + μ(3i + 2j + 6k).

topics.rl: Engineers designing a cable-stayed bridge can find the angle between two cables in 3D from their direction vectors, using exactly this formula.

rv.summary: The acute angle between two lines is given by cos θ = |b₁ · b₂|/(|b₁||b₂|). Lines are perpendicular when a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0 and parallel when their direction ratios are proportional.
focus: Find the angle between two lines
Find an unknown for perpendicular lines
Recognise parallel lines
remember: cos θ = |a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂| / (√(a₁² + b₁² + c₁²)√(a₂² + b₂² + c₂²))
traps: Use directions, not points
Multiply the magnitudes, don't multiply the squares
Keep the modulus for the acute angle

topics.h: Two flyovers cross at different heights without meeting. How close do they get? That gap is the shortest distance between skew lines.
p: Skew lines are lines in space that are neither parallel nor intersecting (they lie in different planes).
The shortest distance is along the segment perpendicular to both lines.
For r = a₁ + λb₁ and r = a₂ + μb₂: d = |(a₂ − a₁) · (b₁ × b₂)| / |b₁ × b₂|.
Cartesian form: d = |det[[x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁], [a₁, b₁, c₁], [a₂, b₂, c₂]]| / √[(b₁c₂ − b₂c₁)² + (c₁a₂ − c₂a₁)² + (a₁b₂ − a₂b₁)²].
If d = 0, the lines intersect.

ex.q: Find the shortest distance between r = i + 2j + k + λ(i − j + k) and r = 2i − j − k + μ(2i + j + 2k).

topics.rl: Air traffic controllers check the closest approach of two straight flight paths that do not meet; if the shortest distance is below the safety limit, one plane is moved to a different path.

rv.summary: Skew lines are neither parallel nor intersecting. Their shortest distance is d = |(a₂ − a₁) · (b₁ × b₂)|/|b₁ × b₂|, and d = 0 means the lines intersect.
focus: Compute b₁ × b₂ and the shortest distance
Decide if two lines are skew or intersecting
remember: Skew: not parallel and not intersecting
traps: Don't stop at the numerator; divide by |b₁ × b₂|
Take the absolute value of the dot product
Watch signs in the cross product

topics.t: Parallel lines and perpendicular lines through a point
topics.h: Two parallel railway tracks never meet, but the gap between them matters. For parallel lines, a simpler distance formula takes over.
p: Parallel lines r = a₁ + λb and r = a₂ + μb: distance d = |b × (a₂ − a₁)| / |b|.
The skew-line formula fails here because b × b = 0.
A line perpendicular to two given lines has direction b₁ × b₂.
Line through a point a perpendicular to both b₁ and b₂: r = a + λ(b₁ × b₂).
Planes, coplanarity of lines, angle between planes and line–plane problems are not in the current CBSE syllabus.

ex.q: Find the distance between r = i + 2j − 4k + λ(2i + 3j + 6k) and r = 3i + 3j − 5k + μ(2i + 3j + 6k).

topics.rl: Indian broad-gauge rails are kept 1676 mm apart. Modelling two straight rails as parallel lines in space, the formula above gives the gap between them.

rv.summary: For parallel lines r = a₁ + λb and r = a₂ + μb, the distance is |b × (a₂ − a₁)|/|b|. A line perpendicular to two given lines has direction b₁ × b₂.
focus: Find the distance between parallel lines
Find a line through a point perpendicular to two lines
Recognise parallel lines from proportional directions
remember: Perpendicular to b₁ and b₂: direction b₁ × b₂
traps: Don't use the skew-line formula for parallel lines (b × b = 0)
Divide by |b|
Don't add the two directions to get a perpendicular one

topics.t: What is a linear programming problem?
topics.h: A furniture dealer in Jodhpur has limited money and limited space. How many tables and chairs should he stock to earn the most? That is a linear programming problem.
p: Linear programming finds the maximum (profit) or minimum (cost) of a linear function under linear restrictions.
Decision variables (x, y) are the quantities we choose. Usually x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (non-negative restrictions).
Objective function: Z = ax + by, to be maximised or minimised.
Constraints: linear inequalities (≤ or ≥) that the variables must satisfy.
Formulating: define variables, write Z, translate each condition into an inequality. (The 'different types of LPP' section is not in the current syllabus.)

ex.q: A dealer buys tables at ₹2500 and chairs at ₹500, with ₹50,000 to spend and space for 60 pieces. Profit is ₹250 per table and ₹75 per chair. Formulate the LPP.
ex.a: Maximise Z = 250x + 75y subject to 5x + y ≤ 100, x + y ≤ 60, x, y ≥ 0

topics.rl: Oil refineries use linear programming to decide how much petrol, diesel and LPG to produce from crude oil so that profit is as large as possible within the plant's limits.

rv.summary: A linear programming problem maximises or minimises a linear objective Z = ax + by subject to linear constraints, usually with x, y ≥ 0. Formulating means naming the variables, writing Z and turning each condition into an inequality.
focus: Identify objective, constraints and decision variables
Translate word conditions into inequalities
Simplify constraints by dividing through
remember: Objective: Z = ax + by (maximise or minimise)
traps: Attach each coefficient to the right variable
Products like xy are not linear
Profit is maximised, cost is minimised

topics.t: Graphing constraints and the feasible region
topics.h: Each constraint cuts the plane in half. Overlap all the allowed halves and you get the feasible region: the only places the answer can live.
p: Each linear inequality ax + by ≤ c represents a half-plane bounded by the line ax + by = c.
To shade the correct side, test a point not on the line (often the origin).
The feasible region is the common region of all constraints (including x, y ≥ 0). Points in it are feasible solutions; points outside are infeasible.
An optimal (feasible) solution is a feasible point that gives the best value of Z.
The corner points of the feasible region are the intersections of its boundary lines.

ex.q: Find the corner points of the region x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
st: x + y = 50 meets the axes at (50, 0) and (0, 50); 3x + y = 90 at (30, 0) and (0, 90).
The origin satisfies both, so shade towards it.
Intersection: subtract the equations: 2x = 40, x = 20, y = 30.

topics.rl: A spice exporter can plot weight and budget limits as lines; the overlap of the allowed regions shows every possible shipment mix.

rv.summary: Each linear inequality is a half-plane; test a point such as the origin to choose the side. The feasible region is where all constraints overlap, and its corners are where boundary lines meet.
focus: Shade half-planes correctly
Find corner points by solving boundary equations
Test whether a point is feasible
remember: Test the origin to decide which side to shade
Corner point: intersection of two boundary lines of the region
traps: Check every constraint, not just one, for feasibility
Feasible is not the same as optimal
Don't swap x and y when solving for a corner

topics.h: Among infinitely many feasible points, the best one is always at a corner. So you only need to check a handful of points.
p: Theorem 1: if an LPP has an optimal value, it occurs at a corner point of the feasible region.
Theorem 2: if the feasible region is bounded, Z has both a maximum and a minimum, each at a corner point.
Corner point method: (1) draw the feasible region and find its corners, (2) evaluate Z at each corner, (3) pick the largest (max) or smallest (min) if the region is bounded.
Organise the work in a table: corner point | value of Z.
Always state the answer with the point and the value, e.g. 'maximum Z = 120 at (30, 0)'.

ex.q: Maximise Z = 4x + y subject to x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90, x, y ≥ 0.
st: The region is bounded, so the maximum is the largest value.

topics.rl: A factory planning how many units of two products to make uses the same corner principle: with a linear profit and linear limits, the best plan sits at a corner of the feasible region.

rv.summary: If an LPP has an optimal value, it occurs at a corner point; on a bounded region Z has both a maximum and a minimum there. Evaluate Z at every corner and pick the best.
focus: Make a table of Z at each corner
Find the maximum or minimum and where it occurs
Know Theorems 1 and 2
remember: Theorem 1: optimum (if any) is at a corner
Theorem 2: bounded region ⇒ both max and min exist at corners
State the answer as value and point
traps: Don't assume the intersection corner is always optimal
Evaluate Z at every corner
Compute each Z value carefully

topics.t: Unbounded regions, multiple optima and no solution
topics.h: Sometimes the feasible region runs off to infinity, sometimes two corners tie, and sometimes no point works at all. Each case needs a careful extra check.
p: Unbounded region, minimum candidate m at a corner: m is the minimum only if the open half-plane Z < m has no point in common with the region. For a maximum M, check Z > M.
If that half-plane does meet the region, the optimum does not exist (e.g. no maximum).
Multiple optimal solutions: if two adjacent corners give the same optimal value, every point on the segment joining them is optimal.
No feasible region: if the constraints have no common point, the LPP has no solution.
Word problems (diet, manufacturing, allocation) often give unbounded regions with ≥ constraints; check them carefully.

ex.q: Minimise Z = x + 2y subject to 2x + y ≥ 3, x + 2y ≥ 6, x, y ≥ 0.
st: The region is unbounded with corners (6, 0) and (0, 3).
x + 2y < 6 has no common point with the region (it contradicts x + 2y ≥ 6).
So the minimum 6 is attained at every point of the segment joining (6, 0) and (0, 3).
ex.a: Minimum Z = 6 at all points on the segment from (6, 0) to (0, 3)

topics.rl: Planning a school meal that meets minimum calorie and protein norms (like those set under the PM POSHAN mid-day meal scheme) at the lowest cost is a diet LPP; its ≥ constraints usually give an unbounded feasible region.

rv.summary: On an unbounded region, the best corner value is the optimum only if the open half-plane beyond it misses the region. Equal values at two adjacent corners give infinitely many optimal points, and contradictory constraints give no solution.
focus: Do the half-plane check for unbounded regions
Recognise multiple optimal solutions
Recognise an empty feasible region
remember: Min m is valid if Z < m has no common point with the region
Max M is valid if Z > M has no common point with the region
Two adjacent optimal corners ⇒ every point on the segment is optimal
traps: Don't accept the largest corner value on an unbounded region without checking
Two corners with the same optimum mean infinitely many solutions, not two
Check that the constraints can all hold together

topics.h: The chance of rain today is 30%. But if dark clouds are already rolling in over Mumbai, that chance jumps. New information changes probability: that is conditional probability.
p: Recall: for equally likely outcomes, P(E) = n(E)/n(S); in general 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1 and P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F) − P(E ∩ F).
Conditional probability of E given F: P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F), provided P(F) ≠ 0.
For equally likely outcomes, P(E|F) = n(E ∩ F)/n(F): F becomes the new, reduced sample space.
P(E|F) and P(F|E) are generally different.
Read 'given that', 'if it is known that' as the condition F.

ex.q: A fair die is thrown. Find the probability that it shows 4, given that the number is even.
st: F = even = {2, 4, 6}, so the reduced sample space has 3 outcomes.

topics.rl: Doctors read test results using conditional probability: the chance of a disease given a positive result is very different from the chance of a positive result given the disease.

rv.summary: P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F) is the probability of E when F is known to have happened, with P(F) ≠ 0. For equally likely outcomes, F becomes the new sample space.
focus: Compute P(E|F) from given probabilities
Use the reduced sample space for dice, coins and families
Tell P(E|F) from P(F|E)
traps: Divide by P(F), the given event, not by P(E)
'At least one boy' and 'elder is a boy' give different reduced spaces
Don't use the full sample space after conditioning

topics.h: Conditional probability is a full probability in its own right: it obeys the same rules, just inside the smaller world F.
p: P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) − P((A ∩ B)|F); if A and B are disjoint, the last term is 0.
Typical settings: dice, coins, cards and families with children.
With cards, remember: 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 4 aces/kings/queens/jacks, 26 red and 26 black, 12 face cards.

ex.q: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. Given that it is red, find the probability that it is a king.

topics.rl: Cricket statisticians quote 'probability of winning given the team bats first'. Its complement, the probability of not winning given batting first, is 1 minus that value.

rv.summary: Conditional probability follows the usual rules within F: P(S|F) = 1, the union rule, and P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F).
focus: Use the complement and union rules for conditional probability
Solve card, dice and coin problems with a condition
remember: P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) − P((A ∩ B)|F)
Pack: 52 cards, 13 per suit, 12 face cards, 26 red
traps: Subtract the intersection in the union rule
Use 12 face cards, not 52, when the card is known to be a face card
Don't give P(E|F) when its complement is asked

topics.h: Draw two cards one after the other without putting the first back. The second draw depends on the first, and the multiplication theorem handles that chain.
p: P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F), for P(E), P(F) ≠ 0.
For three events: P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E) P(F|E) P(G|E ∩ F).
Without replacement, the counts change after each draw: numerator and denominator both drop.
Read problems in order: first draw, then second given the first, and so on.
Sanity check: the answer can never be larger than any single probability in the chain.

ex.q: An urn has 10 black and 5 white balls. Two are drawn one after the other without replacement. Find P(both black).

topics.rl: Quality inspectors pick parts without replacement from a lot; the multiplication theorem gives the chance that every part in the sample passes.

rv.summary: P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F|E), and for three events P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F|E)P(G|E ∩ F). Without replacement, the counts change after each draw.
focus: Find probabilities of successive draws without replacement
Use P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F|E)
Extend to three events
remember: Without replacement: reduce both numerator and denominator
traps: Don't keep the same denominator on later draws
Multiply, don't add, for 'and'
Don't assume independence unless told

topics.h: Tossing a coin in Delhi does not change a die roll in Chennai. Such events are independent: knowing one tells you nothing about the other.
p: E and F are independent if P(E|F) = P(E) (with P(F) ≠ 0), equivalently P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F).
Independent is NOT the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive means P(E ∩ F) = 0.
Two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.
E, F, G are mutually independent if P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), P(F ∩ G) = P(F)P(G), P(E ∩ G) = P(E)P(G) and P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F)P(G).
Pairwise independence alone does not guarantee mutual independence.

ex.q: A die is thrown. E = multiple of 3, F = even number. Are E and F independent?
ex.a: Yes, E and F are independent.

topics.rl: Safety systems often use independent backups: if each fails rarely and independently, the chance of all failing together is the product of the small chances, which is tiny.

rv.summary: E and F are independent when P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), i.e. knowing F does not change P(E). Independent events are not the same as mutually exclusive events.
focus: Test independence by comparing P(E ∩ F) and P(E)P(F)
Use independence to find P(A ∩ B) and P(A ∪ B)
Know the conditions for three events
remember: Independent ⇔ P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F) ⇔ P(E|F) = P(E)
Mutual independence of three needs pairwise and triple product rules
traps: Independent does not mean mutually exclusive
Equal probabilities do not prove independence
Pairwise independence is not enough for mutual independence

topics.h: Three bowlers each have a small chance of taking a wicket this over. What is the chance at least one of them does? Flip the question: find the chance none does.
p: If E and F are independent, so are E and F′, E′ and F, and E′ and F′.
P(E′ ∩ F′) = P(E′)P(F′) = (1 − P(E))(1 − P(F)) for independent E, F.
P(at least one of E, F, G) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − P(E′)P(F′)P(G′) for independent events.
With replacement, successive draws are independent; multiply the same probabilities.
To test independence, compare P(E ∩ F) with P(E)P(F).

ex.q: Probabilities that A, B and C hit a target are 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4, independently. Find P(at least one hits).

topics.rl: Disaster managers estimate the chance that at least one of several independent warning systems works, using 1 − P(all fail).

rv.summary: If E and F are independent, so are their complements. 'At least one' is easiest as 1 − P(none), multiplying the complement probabilities for independent events.
focus: Use 1 − P(none) for 'at least one'
Find P(A ∩ B′) and P(A′ ∩ B′) for independent events
Use De Morgan to test independence
traps: Don't add probabilities for 'at least one'
P(E′ ∩ F′) is not 1 − P(E)P(F)
Use P(B′), not P(B), in P(A ∩ B′)

topics.h: A red ball comes out, but which bag did it come from? Bayes' theorem runs probability backwards: from the result to the cause.
p: E₁, E₂, …, Eₙ form a partition of S if they are pairwise disjoint, together make up S, and each has non-zero probability.
Theorem of total probability: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ).
Bayes' theorem: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Eⱼ) P(A|Eⱼ).
Proof idea: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ ∩ A)/P(A); write the top with the multiplication theorem and the bottom with total probability.
The Eᵢ are hypotheses; P(Eᵢ) are prior probabilities and P(Eᵢ|A) are posterior probabilities (after A is observed).

qa.q: If A = {1, 2, 3}, how many relations can be defined on A?
qa.e: A × A has 3 × 3 = 9 ordered pairs, and every subset of A × A is a relation, so there are 2⁹ = 512 relations.

qa.q: If n(A) = 2 and n(B) = 3, how many relations are there from A to B?
qa.e: A × B has 2 × 3 = 6 pairs, so there are 2⁶ = 64 relations from A to B.

qa.q: A = {1, 2, 3} and R = {(a, b): a + b = 10}. What is R?
qa.e: The largest possible sum is 3 + 3 = 6, so no pair satisfies a + b = 10. R = φ.

qa.q: On the set of all people in Mumbai, R = {(a, b): a and b live on planet Earth}. R is
qa.e: Every pair of Mumbai residents lives on Earth, so every pair is in R: R = A × A.

qa.q: Which of these relations from A = {1, 2, 3} to B = {4, 5} is a function?
qa.e: A function needs each element of A to have exactly one image. Only {(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 5)} does this; two elements sharing an image is allowed.

qa.q: f: {1, 2, 3, 4} → {1, 4, 9, 16, 25}, f(x) = x². What is the range of f?
qa.e: The range is the set of actual images: f(1) = 1, f(2) = 4, f(3) = 9, f(4) = 16. 25 is in the codomain but is not an image.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The empty relation on a non-empty set A is a subset of A × A.
Reason (R): The empty set is a subset of every set.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: φ ⊆ every set, in particular φ ⊆ A × A, so φ qualifies as a relation on A. R is exactly why A holds.

qa.q: If n(A) = 4, how many elements does the universal relation on A have?
qa.e: The universal relation is A × A, which has 4 × 4 = 16 ordered pairs.

qa.q: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, which relation is reflexive?
qa.e: Reflexive needs all four pairs (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4). Only the last option contains every one; extra pairs such as (1, 3) do not spoil reflexivity.

qa.q: R on Z defined by a R b ⇔ a − b is an integer. R is
qa.e: a − a = 0 ∈ Z; if a − b ∈ Z then b − a = −(a − b) ∈ Z; and (a − b) + (b − c) = a − c ∈ Z. All three hold.

qa.q: On the set of real numbers, R = {(a, b): a ≤ b²}. Why is R not transitive?
qa.a: (3, −2) and (−2, 1) are in R but (3, 1) is not
qa.e: 3 ≤ (−2)² = 4 and −2 ≤ 1² = 1, but 3 ≤ 1² is false. One counter-example breaks transitivity.

qa.q: On A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)}. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: R is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
qa.e: Reverse pairs are present, so R is symmetric. (1, 1) ∉ R, so not reflexive. (1, 2), (2, 1) ∈ R needs (1, 1), so not transitive.

qa.q: On the set of lines in a plane, R = {(L1, L2): L1 ⊥ L2}. R is
qa.a: symmetric but not reflexive or transitive
qa.e: If L1 ⊥ L2 then L2 ⊥ L1. No line is perpendicular to itself, and L1 ⊥ L2, L2 ⊥ L3 make L1 parallel to L3, not perpendicular.

qa.q: R on N: a R b ⇔ b is divisible by a. Which property fails?
qa.e: a | a, and a | b, b | c give a | c. But 2 | 4 while 4 ∤ 2, so R is not symmetric.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): R = {(1, 1), (2, 2)} on A = {1, 2, 3} is reflexive.
Reason (R): R contains (a, a) for some a in A.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: Reflexive needs (a, a) for every a; (3, 3) is missing, so A is false. R is a true statement about this relation, but 'some' is not enough.

qa.q: What is the least number of ordered pairs that must be added to R = {(1, 2), (2, 3)} on A = {1, 2, 3} to make it reflexive and transitive?
qa.e: Reflexive needs (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3). Transitive needs (1, 3) because of (1, 2) and (2, 3). That is 4 pairs, and the new set is transitive.

qa.q: Which of these relations on A = {1, 2, 3} is an equivalence relation?
qa.e: {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 3), (3, 1)} is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The first option is not symmetric ((1, 2) without (2, 1)), the third misses (3, 3), and the last has (1, 2), (2, 3) without (1, 3).

qa.q: For congruence modulo 3 on Z, how many distinct equivalence classes are there?
qa.e: Every integer leaves remainder 0, 1 or 2 on division by 3, so the classes are [0], [1], [2].

qa.q: On Z, R = {(a, b): 2 divides a − b}. The equivalence class [1] is
qa.a: the set of all odd integers
qa.e: x R 1 means x − 1 is even, i.e. x is odd. So [1] = {…, −3, −1, 1, 3, …}.

qa.q: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}, R = {(a, b): a − b is even}. How many elements are in [2]?
qa.e: x − 2 is even exactly when x is even: x = 2, 4, 6. So [2] has 3 elements.

qa.q: How many equivalence relations on A = {1, 2, 3} contain the pair (1, 2)?
qa.e: Smallest one: {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1)}. Adding any pair with 3, e.g. (2, 3), forces all pairs, giving the universal relation. So exactly 2.

qa.q: Two equivalence classes [a] and [b] of an equivalence relation have a common element. What can you conclude?
qa.e: If c is in both, then c R a and c R b, so a R b by symmetry and transitivity. Then every element of one class lies in the other, so the classes are equal.

qa.q: R on the set of all triangles in a plane: T1 R T2 ⇔ T1 is similar to T2. R is
qa.e: Every triangle is similar to itself, similarity is mutual, and similarity passes along a chain. So R is an equivalence relation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The relation 'a R b ⇔ |a − b| is even' on A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} has exactly 2 equivalence classes.
Reason (R): Every element of A is either even or odd, and two numbers differ by an even number only if both have the same parity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The classes are {1, 3, 5} and {2, 4}. R gives the reason: elements of the same parity are related, different parity are not.

qa.q: f: N → N, f(x) = 2x. Which is true?
qa.e: 2x1 = 2x2 ⇒ x1 = x2, so one-one. Odd numbers like 1 have no pre-image in N, so not onto.

qa.q: f: R → R, f(x) = x². Why is f not one-one?
qa.e: Two different inputs −3 and 3 give the same output 9, so f is many-one.

qa.q: f: R → R, f(x) = x². Why is f not onto?
qa.e: Negative numbers in the codomain are never outputs of x², so range ≠ codomain.

qa.q: Which function from R to R is bijective?
qa.e: x³ is strictly increasing (one-one) and every real y has the real cube root ∛y as pre-image (onto).

qa.q: f: N → N, f(n) = (n + 1)/2 if n is odd and n/2 if n is even. f is
qa.e: f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 1, so not one-one. For any m ∈ N, f(2m) = m, so onto.

qa.q: f: R − {0} → R, f(x) = 1/x. Which is true?
qa.e: 1/x1 = 1/x2 ⇒ x1 = x2, so one-one. But 0 in the codomain is never equal to 1/x, so not onto.

qa.q: For f: A → A on a finite set A, which statement is always true?
qa.a: f is one-one if and only if f is onto
qa.e: On a finite set mapped to itself, distinct inputs filling distinct outputs uses up all the elements, and vice versa. So one-one ⇔ onto.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): f: Z → Z, f(x) = x + 1 is a bijection.
Reason (R): Every one-one function is onto.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: x + 1 is one-one, and y has pre-image y − 1 in Z, so A is true. R is false: f(x) = 2x on N is one-one but not onto.

qa.q: f: R → R, f(x) = [x], the greatest integer function. f is
qa.e: [1.2] = [1.7] = 1, so not one-one. The range is Z, so 0.5 has no pre-image and f is not onto.

qa.q: f: R → R, f(x) = |x|. Which is true?
qa.e: |−1| = |1| makes it many-one, and negative numbers are never values of |x|, so not onto.

qa.q: How many one-one functions are there from A = {1, 2, 3} to B = {a, b, c, d}?
qa.e: 1 has 4 choices, 2 then has 3, and 3 has 2: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.

qa.q: How many onto functions are there from {1, 2, 3, 4} to {a, b}?
qa.e: There are 2⁴ = 16 functions. Remove the 2 constant functions (all to a, all to b). 16 − 2 = 14.

qa.q: How many bijective functions are there from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} to itself?
qa.e: A bijection on n elements is an arrangement of them: 5! = 120.

qa.q: f: N → N, f(x) = x + 1 if x is odd, x − 1 if x is even. f is
qa.e: f swaps 1↔2, 3↔4, 5↔6, … Odd inputs give even outputs and even inputs give odd outputs, with no clashes, and every n is hit. So f is a bijection.

qa.q: How many one-one functions are there from a set with 4 elements to a set with 3 elements?
qa.e: There are only 3 possible images for 4 inputs, so two inputs must share an image. No one-one function exists.

qa.q: Which function from N to N is one-one but not onto?
qa.e: x² is one-one on N (positive inputs), but 2 is not a perfect square, so not onto. f(x) = x and |x| are bijective on N; the last one sends 1 and 2 to 1.

qa.q: What is the principal value branch (range) of sin⁻¹ x?
qa.e: Sine is restricted to [−π/2, π/2], where it is one-one and takes every value in [−1, 1].

qa.q: What is the principal value branch of cos⁻¹ x?
qa.e: Cosine is one-one on [0, π] and covers [−1, 1] there, so cos⁻¹ takes values in [0, π].

qa.q: What is the domain of cos⁻¹(x − 1)?
qa.e: We need −1 ≤ x − 1 ≤ 1, so 0 ≤ x ≤ 2.

qa.q: What is the domain of sin⁻¹(2x)?
Why must sin x be restricted before we define sin⁻¹ x?
qa.a: Because sin x is not one-one on R
qa.e: An inverse needs a bijection. On R, sine repeats values, so it is many-one; restricting to [−π/2, π/2] fixes this.

qa.q: Which expression equals cosec x?
qa.e: (sin x)⁻¹ means 1/sin x, which is cosec x. sin⁻¹ x is an angle, not a reciprocal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): sin⁻¹(3/2) is not defined.
Reason (R): The range of sin⁻¹ x is [−π/2, π/2].
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: A is true because 3/2 is outside the domain [−1, 1]. R is a true fact about the range, but the reason for A is the domain, not the range.

qa.q: If y = cos⁻¹ x, which pair of statements is correct?
qa.a: cos y = x and 0 ≤ y ≤ π
qa.e: y is the angle in [0, π] whose cosine is x.

qa.q: What is the domain of sec⁻¹ x?
qa.e: sec x never lies strictly between −1 and 1, so sec⁻¹ is defined only for x ≤ −1 or x ≥ 1.

qa.q: What is the range of cot⁻¹ x?
qa.e: cot is one-one on (0, π) and takes every real value there; the end points are excluded because cot is undefined at 0 and π.

qa.q: Which value is NOT in the range of cosec⁻¹ x?
qa.e: cosec⁻¹ x takes values in [−π/2, π/2] except 0, because cosec 0 is undefined.

qa.q: Why is π/2 excluded from the range of sec⁻¹ x?
qa.e: sec x = 1/cos x and cos(π/2) = 0, so sec(π/2) does not exist; no x has sec⁻¹ x = π/2.

qa.q: The graph of y = cos⁻¹ x passes through which point?
qa.e: cos⁻¹(−1) = π, since cos π = −1 and π is in [0, π]. The graph runs from (−1, π) down to (1, 0).

qa.q: How is the graph of y = tan⁻¹ x obtained from y = tan x on (−π/2, π/2)?
qa.a: By reflecting it in the line y = x
qa.e: The graph of an inverse is the mirror image of the original in y = x; swapping coordinates swaps domain and range.

qa.q: As x → ∞, tan⁻¹ x approaches
qa.e: tan θ → ∞ as θ → π/2 from the left, so tan⁻¹ x → π/2 but never reaches it.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): tan⁻¹ x is defined for every real number x.
Reason (R): tan x takes every real value on (−π/2, π/2).
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because restricted tan is onto R, its inverse accepts every real input. R directly explains A.

qa.q: What is the principal value of cos⁻¹(−√3/2)?
qa.e: cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹ x, so cos⁻¹(−√3/2) = π − π/6 = 5π/6, which lies in [0, π].

qa.q: What is the principal value of sec⁻¹(−2)?
qa.e: sec θ = −2 means cos θ = −1/2. In [0, π] − {π/2}, θ = 2π/3.

qa.q: What is the principal value of cosec⁻¹(−√2)?
qa.e: cosec θ = −√2 means sin θ = −1/√2. In [−π/2, π/2] − {0}, θ = −π/4.

qa.q: Evaluate cos⁻¹(1/2) + 2 sin⁻¹(1/2).
qa.e: cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3 and sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6, so the sum is π/3 + 2(π/6) = 2π/3.

qa.q: Evaluate tan⁻¹(√3) − sec⁻¹(−2).
qa.e: tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3 and sec⁻¹(−2) = 2π/3, so the difference is π/3 − 2π/3 = −π/3.

qa.q: What is the principal value of tan⁻¹(−1)?
qa.e: tan⁻¹ is odd: tan⁻¹(−1) = −tan⁻¹(1) = −π/4, which lies in (−π/2, π/2).

qa.q: What is the principal value of cot⁻¹(−√3)?
qa.e: cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹ x, so the value is π − π/6 = 5π/6, inside (0, π).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): sin⁻¹(−1/2) = 7π/6.
Reason (R): sin(7π/6) = −1/2.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: sin(7π/6) is indeed −1/2, but 7π/6 is not in [−π/2, π/2]. The principal value is −π/6, so A is false.

qa.q: Evaluate sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3).
qa.e: sin(2π/3) = sin(π − π/3) = sin(π/3), and π/3 is in [−π/2, π/2]. So the value is π/3.

qa.q: Evaluate cos⁻¹(cos 7π/6).
qa.e: cos(7π/6) = −√3/2 and cos⁻¹(−√3/2) = 5π/6, which lies in [0, π].

qa.q: Evaluate tan⁻¹[2 cos(2 sin⁻¹(1/2))].
Evaluate sin[π/3 − sin⁻¹(−1/2)].
qa.e: sin⁻¹(−1/2) = −π/6, so the angle is π/3 + π/6 = π/2, and sin(π/2) = 1.

qa.q: For −π/2 < x < π/2, tan⁻¹[cos x/(1 − sin x)] simplifies to
qa.e: cos x/(1 − sin x) = (cos(x/2) + sin(x/2))/(cos(x/2) − sin(x/2)) = tan(π/4 + x/2), and π/4 + x/2 lies in (0, π/2).

qa.q: For |x| < a, tan⁻¹[x/√(a² − x²)] equals
qa.e: Put x = a sin θ: √(a² − x²) = a cos θ, so the ratio is tan θ and the expression is θ = sin⁻¹(x/a).

qa.q: For x ∈ (0, π), tan⁻¹√[(1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x)] equals
qa.e: (1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x) = tan²(x/2), and tan(x/2) > 0 for x ∈ (0, π), so the expression is tan⁻¹(tan x/2) = x/2.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): sin⁻¹(sin 3π/5) = 2π/5.
Reason (R): sin⁻¹(sin x) = x for all x in [−π/2, π/2].
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: sin(3π/5) = sin(π − 3π/5) = sin(2π/5), and 2π/5 lies in [−π/2, π/2]; by R the answer is 2π/5.

qa.q: How many possible orders can a matrix with 24 elements have?
qa.e: 24 has divisors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, and each gives one order d × (24/d): 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6 and their reverses.

qa.q: A matrix has 18 elements. How many possible orders does it have?
qa.e: Divisors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, giving 6 orders.

qa.q: For a 2 × 2 matrix with aij = (i + j)²/2, what is a12?
For a 3 × 2 matrix with aij = |−3i + j|/2, what is a31?
In the matrix A = [[2, 5, −1], [7, 0, 3]], what is a23?
qa.e: a23 is row 2, column 3: the third entry of [7, 0, 3], which is 3.

qa.q: What is the order of A = [[2, 5, −1], [7, 0, 3]]?
qa.e: It has 2 rows and 3 columns.

qa.q: How many 3 × 3 matrices can be formed with each entry 0 or 1?
qa.e: There are 9 entries, each with 2 choices: 2⁹ = 512.

qa.q: A 1 × n matrix that lists the prices of n items in a canteen is best described as
qa.e: One row and n columns is a row matrix.

qa.q: Which matrix is a scalar matrix?
qa.e: A scalar matrix is diagonal with all diagonal entries equal. Only [[−2, 0], [0, −2]] qualifies.

qa.q: Which statement is true?
qa.a: Every identity matrix is a scalar matrix
qa.e: I is diagonal with all diagonal entries 1, so it is scalar. Scalar matrices like 3I are not identity, and zero matrices can be any order.

qa.q: If [[x + y, 2], [5, xy]] = [[6, 2], [5, 8]], which values satisfy the equation?
qa.e: x + y = 6 and xy = 8 give the numbers 2 and 4 in either order.
2a + b = 4 and a − 2b = −3. Multiply the first by 2 and add: 5a = 5, so a = 1 (and b = 2).

qa.q: Using the same equation [[2a + b, a − 2b], [5c − d, 4c + 3d]] = [[4, −3], [11, 24]], find d.
qa.e: 5c − d = 11 and 4c + 3d = 24. Multiply the first by 3 and add: 19c = 57, so c = 3, then d = 15 − 11 = 4.

qa.q: A diagonal matrix of order 3 has how many elements that MUST be zero?
qa.e: A 3 × 3 matrix has 9 elements; the 3 diagonal ones are free, so the other 6 must be zero.

qa.q: Can the matrices [[1, 2]] and [[1], [2]] be equal?
qa.a: No, because their orders are different
qa.e: Equality needs the same order. One is 1 × 2 and the other is 2 × 1, so they cannot be equal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): [[0, 0, 0]] is a zero matrix.
Reason (R): A zero matrix must be a square matrix.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: All entries are 0, so it is a 1 × 3 zero matrix. Zero matrices can be of any order, so R is false.

qa.q: If A = [[3, −1], [2, 4]] and B = [[1, 5], [−2, 0]], what is the sum of all entries of A + B?
qa.e: A + B = [[4, 4], [0, 4]], whose entries add to 12.
Adding the equations gives 2X = [[10, 0], [2, 8]], so X = [[5, 0], [1, 4]].

qa.q: For the same pair X + Y = [[7, 0], [2, 5]] and X − Y = [[3, 0], [0, 3]], what is Y?
Which is the additive inverse of A = [[2, −3], [0, 1]]?
qa.e: The additive inverse is −A, which changes the sign of every entry; A + (−A) = O.

qa.q: If A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 2, which expression is defined?
qa.e: A scalar multiple is defined for any matrix. A + B needs equal orders, and 2 × 3 ≠ 3 × 2.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): If A and B are 2 × 2 matrices, then 3(A + B) = 3A + 3B.
Reason (R): Matrix addition is commutative.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: A holds because scalar multiplication distributes over addition. Commutativity is true but is a different property.
Row 1 of A is (1, 2) and column 2 of B is (0, 3): 1·0 + 2·3 = 6.

qa.q: For the same A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[2, 0], [1, 3]], what is the (2, 2) entry of BA?
qa.e: Row 2 of B is (1, 3) and column 2 of A is (2, 4): 1·2 + 3·4 = 14. (The (2, 2) entry of AB is 12, showing AB ≠ BA.)

qa.q: A is 3 × 2 and B is 2 × 5. How many elements does AB have?
qa.e: AB has order 3 × 5, which has 15 elements.

qa.q: If A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 2, which statement is true?
qa.a: Both AB and BA are defined, but they have different orders
qa.e: AB is 2 × 2 and BA is 3 × 3, so both exist but cannot be equal.

qa.q: If A = [[2, 0], [0, 2]], what is A³?

Assertion (A): For square matrices A and B of the same order, (A + B)² = A² + 2AB + B² always.
Reason (R): Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², which equals A² + 2AB + B² only if AB = BA. Since that fails in general (R), A is false.

qa.q: If A is a 3 × 5 matrix, what is the order of A′?
qa.e: Transposing swaps rows and columns.

qa.q: Which of the following equals (AB)′?
qa.e: The transpose of a product reverses the order: (AB)′ = B′A′.

qa.q: A is skew-symmetric of order 3 with a12 = 4 and a13 = −2. What is a31?
qa.e: Skew-symmetric means a31 = −a13 = −(−2) = 2.

For A = [[1, 5], [7, 2]], the skew-symmetric part (1/2)(A − A′) is
How many entries of a 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrix can be chosen freely?
qa.e: Diagonal entries are forced to 0, and the 3 entries below the diagonal are negatives of the 3 above. So only 3 are free.

qa.q: If A is symmetric and B is any square matrix of the same order, then B′AB is

qa.e: r = 6h, so V = (1/3)π(36h²)h = 12πh³. dV/dt = 36πh² dh/dt ⇒ 12 = 36π(16) dh/dt ⇒ dh/dt = 1/(48π).

qa.q: A balloon stays spherical. Its radius grows at 0.5 cm/s. How fast (cm³/s) is its volume growing when r = 2 cm, in terms of π?
qa.e: dV/dt = 4πr² dr/dt = 4π(4)(0.5) = 8π cm³/s.

qa.q: A man 2 m tall walks away from a 6 m lamp post at 5 km/h. Taking x as his distance from the post and s as his shadow length, which relation follows from similar triangles?
qa.e: Lamp height 6 over (x + s) equals man's height 2 over s: 6s = 2x + 2s ⇒ s = x/2. Then ds/dt = (1/2)(5) = 2.5 km/h.

qa.q: What does a marginal cost of ₹45 at x = 10 units mean?
qa.a: Producing the 11th unit costs about ₹45 more
qa.e: Marginal cost is the instantaneous rate of change of total cost, approximately the extra cost of one more unit.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When the foot of a sliding ladder moves away from the wall, dy/dt for the top is negative.
Reason (R): x dx/dt + y dy/dt = 0 with x, y, dx/dt > 0 forces dy/dt < 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Since x dx/dt > 0 and y > 0, we need dy/dt < 0 to make the sum zero, which is why the top moves down.

qa.q: Which function is strictly decreasing on R?
qa.e: f′(x) = −3 < 0 for all x.

qa.q: On which interval is f(x) = sin x strictly decreasing?
qa.e: f′(x) = cos x < 0 on (π/2, π).

qa.q: Why is f(x) = x³ strictly increasing on R even though f′(0) = 0?
qa.a: Because f′(x) > 0 except at a single point, and x1 < x2 still gives x1³ < x2³
qa.e: f′(x) = 3x² ≥ 0 and vanishes only at x = 0; the definition x1 < x2 ⇒ x1³ < x2³ holds everywhere.

qa.q: Which statement about f(x) = log x is true?
f(x) = cos x on (0, π) is

qa.q: Is f(x) = x² increasing at x = 0?
qa.a: No; it is neither increasing nor decreasing at 0
qa.e: In every interval around 0, f decreases on the left and increases on the right, so it is neither.

qa.q: For which value of k is f(x) = kx + 7 strictly increasing on R?
qa.e: f′(x) = k must be positive, so k = 2 works and the others do not.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): f(x) = e^(−x) is strictly decreasing on R.
Reason (R): f′(x) = −e^(−x) < 0 for all x.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Since eᵗ > 0 always, the derivative −e^(−x) is always negative, which is why f strictly decreases.

qa.q: On which interval is f(x) = x² − 4x + 6 strictly increasing?
qa.e: f′(x) = 2x − 4 > 0 when x > 2.

qa.q: On which interval is f(x) = x³ − 3x strictly decreasing?
For f(x) = −2x³ − 9x² − 12x + 1, on which interval is f strictly increasing?
qa.e: f′(x) = −6x² − 18x − 12 = −6(x + 1)(x + 2). This is positive between −2 and −1.

qa.q: Find the least value of a such that f(x) = x² + ax + 1 is strictly increasing on (1, 2).
qa.e: f′(x) = 2x + a > 0 on (1, 2) needs 2(1) + a ≥ 0, so a ≥ −2. The least value is −2.

qa.q: On [0, 2π], where is f(x) = sin x + cos x strictly increasing?
qa.e: f′(x) = cos x − sin x = 0 at π/4 and 5π/4. f′ > 0 on [0, π/4) and (5π/4, 2π].

qa.q: Which statement about f(x) = x/2 + 2/x (x ≠ 0) is correct?
qa.a: It is strictly decreasing on (−2, 0) and (0, 2)

qa.q: Show that f(x) = log(sin x) is strictly increasing on (0, π/2). Which is the key reason?
qa.e: f′(x) = cos x/sin x = cot x, which is positive in the first quadrant.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 12x − 18 is increasing on R.
Reason (R): f′(x) = 3(x − 2)² ≥ 0 for all real x.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 12 = 3(x − 2)², which is never negative, so f is increasing on R (in fact strictly).

qa.q: Which point is a critical point of f(x) = |x|?
qa.a: x = 0, where f′ does not exist
qa.e: Critical points include points where f′ does not exist. |x| has a corner at 0, and that is its minimum.

qa.q: For f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 15, what is the local maximum value?
qa.e: Critical points 1 and 3; f′ changes + to − at 1. f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 15 = 19.

qa.q: For f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 15, what is the local minimum value?
qa.e: At x = 3, f′ changes − to +, so f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 + 15 = 15 is a local minimum.

qa.q: What kind of point is x = 0 for f(x) = x³?
qa.a: A point of inflection, neither max nor min
qa.e: f′(0) = 0 but f′ = 3x² ≥ 0 on both sides, so no sign change: neither maximum nor minimum.

qa.q: What is the minimum value of f(x) = 9x² + 12x + 2?
Does f(x) = eˣ have a local maximum or minimum on R?
qa.e: f′(x) = eˣ is never zero and always exists, so there are no critical points and no local extrema.

qa.q: For f(x) = x⁴ − 62x² + ax + 9 to have a local maximum at x = 1, what must a be?
qa.e: f′(1) = 4 − 124 + a = 0 ⇒ a = 120. (Then f″(1) = 12 − 124 < 0, confirming a maximum.)

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Every local maximum value of a function is greater than every local minimum value.
Reason (R): At a local maximum, f′ changes from positive to negative.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: 'Local' means only nearby comparison. A wavy function can have a local max lower than a local min elsewhere, so A is false. R is the correct sign-change rule.

qa.q: For f(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 36x + 1 on [1, 5], what is the absolute maximum value?
qa.e: Values: f(1) = 24, f(2) = 29, f(3) = 28, f(5) = 56. The largest is at the end point 5.

qa.q: Find the absolute minimum of f(x) = x² on [−2, 1].
qa.e: Critical point x = 0 gives 0; end points give 4 and 1. The smallest is 0.

qa.q: Find the absolute maximum of f(x) = 4x − x²/2 on [−2, 9/2].
For the same f(x) = 4x − x²/2 on [−2, 9/2], what is the absolute minimum?
qa.e: f(−2) = −8 − 2 = −10 is the smallest of −10, 8 and 63/8.

qa.q: Using the second derivative test, x = 1 for f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 15 is
qa.e: f″(x) = 6x − 12, so f″(1) = −6 < 0: local maximum.

qa.q: What does the second derivative test say about f(x) = x⁴ at x = 0?
qa.a: It fails because f″(0) = 0; the first derivative test shows a minimum
qa.e: f′(0) = 0 and f″(0) = 0, so the test is inconclusive. f′ = 4x³ changes − to +, giving a minimum.

qa.q: Find the maximum value of f(x) = sin x + cos x on [0, π].
qa.e: f′ = cos x − sin x = 0 at π/4, where f = √2. f(0) = 1, f(π) = −1. Max is √2.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The absolute maximum of f(x) = x on [0, 3] is at x = 3.
Reason (R): f has no critical points in (0, 3), so the extreme values occur at end points.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: f′ = 1 ≠ 0, so only end points matter: f(0) = 0, f(3) = 3. R explains A.

qa.q: Two positive numbers have sum 24. What is their maximum product?
qa.e: P = x(24 − x), P′ = 24 − 2x = 0 at x = 12. P = 12 × 12 = 144; P″ = −2 < 0 confirms a maximum.

qa.q: Two positive numbers have sum 16. What is the minimum possible sum of their cubes?
From an 18 cm square sheet, an open box is made by cutting equal squares from the corners. What is the maximum volume (cm³)?
qa.e: V = x(18 − 2x)² is maximum at x = 3, giving V = 3 × 144 = 432.

qa.q: Find the point on the curve x² = 2y nearest to (0, 5).
A rectangle is inscribed in a circle of radius 5 cm. What is the maximum possible area (cm²)?
qa.e: The maximum rectangle is a square with diagonal 10, so side 5√2 and area 50 = 2r².

qa.q: Profit P(x) = −x² + 40x − 100 (₹ thousand). For which output x is profit maximum?
qa.e: P′ = −2x + 40 = 0 ⇒ x = 20, and P″ = −2 < 0. (Maximum profit is 300 thousand.)

qa.q: For the same profit P(x) = −x² + 40x − 100 (₹ thousand), what is the maximum profit?
A closed cylindrical can must hold a fixed volume with the least metal. What is the relation between its height h and radius r?
qa.e: S = 2πr² + 2V/r. S′ = 4πr − 2V/r² = 0 ⇒ V = 2πr³, and V = πr²h gives h = 2r.

qa.q: What is ∫(3x² − 4x + 5) dx?
qa.e: Integrate term by term: x³ − 2x² + 5x + C.

qa.q: What is ∫(√x + 1/√x) dx?
What is ∫(2 − 3 sin x)/cos²x dx?
qa.e: Split: 2 sec²x − 3 sec x tan x. Integrate: 2 tan x − 3 sec x + C.

qa.q: f′(x) = 3x² + 2x and f(1) = 5. What is f(2)?
Which function is an anti-derivative of sin 2x?
What is ∫(x³ − 1)/(x − 1) dx?
qa.e: (x³ − 1)/(x − 1) = x² + x + 1, which integrates to x³/3 + x²/2 + x + C.

qa.q: What is ∫eˣ(1 + e⁻ˣ) dx?
qa.e: eˣ(1 + e⁻ˣ) = eˣ + 1, whose integral is eˣ + x + C.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): ∫(1/x) dx = log|x| + C for x ≠ 0.
Reason (R): The power rule ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C works for n = −1.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is a standard result. R is false: at n = −1 the power rule would divide by zero.

qa.q: What is ∫2x cos(x²) dx?
qa.e: Put t = x², dt = 2x dx: ∫cos t dt = sin t + C = sin(x²) + C.

qa.q: What is ∫sin(3x + 5) dx?
qa.e: Put t = 3x + 5, dt = 3 dx: (1/3)∫sin t dt = −(1/3) cos t + C.

qa.q: What is ∫e^(tan⁻¹ x)/(1 + x²) dx?
qa.e: With t = tan⁻¹ x, dt = dx/(1 + x²), the integral is ∫eᵗ dt.

qa.q: What is ∫(2x + 3)/(x² + 3x + 7) dx?
qa.e: The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so it is ∫f′/f = log|f| + C.

qa.q: What is ∫tan x dx?
qa.e: tan x = sin x/cos x = −(−sin x)/cos x, so ∫tan x dx = −log|cos x| = log|sec x| + C.

Reason (R): cot x = cos x/sin x and d/dx(sin x) = cos x.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: cot x has the form f′/f with f = sin x, so its integral is log|sin x| + C.

qa.q: What is ∫sin²x dx?
qa.e: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, so the integral is x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C.

qa.q: What is ∫cos²x dx?
qa.e: cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2, giving x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + C.

qa.q: What is ∫tan²x dx?
qa.e: tan²x = sec²x − 1, so ∫ = tan x − x + C.

qa.q: What is ∫sin 2x cos 3x dx?
qa.e: sin 2x cos 3x = (1/2)(sin 5x − sin x). Integrating: (1/2)(−cos 5x/5 + cos x).

qa.q: What is ∫sin³x dx?
qa.e: sin³x = (3 sin x − sin 3x)/4; integrate each term.

qa.q: What is ∫cos 2x cos 4x dx?
qa.e: cos 2x cos 4x = (1/2)[cos 6x + cos 2x]. Integrate: (1/2)[sin 6x/6 + sin 2x/2] = sin 6x/12 + sin 2x/4.

qa.q: What is ∫(1 − cos 2x)/(1 + cos 2x) dx?
qa.e: (1 − cos 2x)/(1 + cos 2x) = 2 sin²x/(2 cos²x) = tan²x = sec²x − 1.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): ∫cos³x dx = sin x − (sin³x)/3 + C.
Reason (R): cos³x = (1 − sin²x) cos x, and t = sin x gives ∫(1 − t²) dt.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: With t = sin x, ∫(1 − t²) dt = t − t³/3 + C, which is A.

qa.q: What is ∫dx/(x² + 16)?
What is ∫dx/√(1 − 4x²)?
What is ∫dx/(x² − 9)?
What is ∫dx/(9 − x²)?
qa.e: ∫dx/(a² − x²) = (1/2a) log|(a + x)/(a − x)| with a = 3.

What is ∫x²/(1 − x⁶) dx?

Reason (R): ∫dx/√(a² − x²) = (1/a) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: The correct formula is ∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C, with no 1/a. So A is true and R is false.

To find ∫(x + 2)/(2x² + 6x + 5) dx, we write x + 2 = A(4x + 6) + B. What is A?

qa.q: For the same split x + 2 = A(4x + 6) + B, what is B?
qa.e: Constants: 6A + B = 2 ⇒ 6/4 + B = 2 ⇒ B = 1/2.

qa.q: What is ∫dx/√(x² + 4x − 5)?
qa.e: x² + 4x − 5 = (x + 2)² − 3², so the form ∫dt/√(t² − a²) gives log|t + √(t² − a²)| + C.

qa.q: What is ∫(2x + 1)/√(x² + x + 1) dx?
qa.e: Put t = x² + x + 1, dt = (2x + 1) dx: ∫t^(−1/2) dt = 2√t + C.

qa.q:

Reason (R): ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The A part becomes an f′/f integral, which R handles directly; that is why we split this way.

qa.q: What is ∫dx/((x + 1)(x + 2))?
qa.e: 1/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = 1/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 2), which integrates to log|x + 1| − log|x + 2|.

qa.q: For the same decomposition, what is C?
Which partial-fraction form is correct for (x² + 1)/((x − 1)(x² + 4))?
qa.e: x² + 4 cannot be factored over reals, so its numerator must be linear, Bx + C.

qa.e: The numerator's degree equals the denominator's, so divide first; then split the proper part.

qa.e: u = x, v = eˣ: x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C.

qa.q: What is ∫log x dx?
qa.e: Take log x as u and 1 as v: x log x − ∫x · (1/x) dx = x log x − x + C.

qa.q: What is ∫x log x dx?
qa.e: u = log x (L before A): (x²/2) log x − ∫(x²/2)(1/x) dx = (x²/2) log x − x²/4 + C.

qa.q: What is ∫sin⁻¹x dx?
qa.e: x sin⁻¹x − ∫x/√(1 − x²) dx, and ∫x/√(1 − x²) dx = −√(1 − x²), so the result is x sin⁻¹x + √(1 − x²) + C.

qa.q: What is ∫eˣ sin x dx?
qa.e: Parts twice gives I = eˣ sin x − eˣ cos x − I, so 2I = eˣ(sin x − cos x).

qa.q: What is ∫x² eˣ dx?
qa.e: Parts: x²eˣ − 2∫x eˣ dx = x²eˣ − 2eˣ(x − 1) + C = eˣ(x² − 2x + 2) + C.

qa.q: Which choice of first function is right for ∫x sec²x dx?
qa.a: x, giving x tan x − log|sec x| + C
qa.e: A comes before T in ILATE. ∫x sec²x dx = x tan x − ∫tan x dx = x tan x − log|sec x| + C.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In ∫x eˣ dx we take x as the first function.
Reason (R): In ILATE, algebraic functions come before exponential functions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Differentiating x makes it simpler while eˣ is easy to integrate; ILATE encodes this choice.

qa.q: What is ∫eˣ(sin x + cos x) dx?
qa.e: With f = sin x, f′ = cos x, the integral is eˣ f(x) + C.

qa.q: What is ∫eˣ(1/x − 1/x²) dx?
qa.e: f(x) = 1/x has f′(x) = −1/x², so the answer is eˣ/x + C.

qa.q: What is ∫eˣ(x − 1)/x² dx?
qa.e: (x − 1)/x² = 1/x − 1/x², which is f + f′ with f = 1/x.

qa.q: What is ∫√(4 − x²) dx?
What is ∫√(x² + 9) dx?
qa.e: Use the √(x² + a²) formula with a = 3; the log term has a plus sign.

qa.q: What is ∫√(x² − 16) dx?
qa.e: a² = 16, so the log term is −(16/2) = −8 times log|x + √(x² − 16)|.

qa.q: What is ∫eˣ(sec x)(1 + tan x) dx?
qa.e: sec x(1 + tan x) = sec x + sec x tan x, and d/dx(sec x) = sec x tan x. So f = sec x.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): ∫eˣ(x + 1) dx = x eˣ + C.
Reason (R): d/dx(x eˣ) = eˣ(x + 1).
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: By the product rule, d/dx(x eˣ) = eˣ + x eˣ = eˣ(x + 1). That is the f + f′ pattern with f = x.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀² (x² + 1) dx.
Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) cos x dx.

Evaluate ∫₁^e log x dx.
If F(x) = ∫₀ˣ cos t dt, what is F′(π/3)?
qa.e: By the first fundamental theorem, F′(x) = cos x, so F′(π/3) = cos(π/3) = 1/2.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₂³ dx/(x² − 1).

Assertion (A): ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2.
Reason (R): The anti-derivative of sin x is −cos x, so the integral is −cos π + cos 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: −cos π + cos 0 = 1 + 1 = 2. R is the fundamental-theorem calculation behind A.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x/(x² + 1) dx.
qa.e: t = x² + 1, dt = 2x dx, limits 1 to 2: (1/2)∫₁² dt/t = (1/2) log 2.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ tan⁻¹x/(1 + x²) dx.
qa.e: t = tan⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/4: ∫t dt = (π/4)²/2 = π²/32.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ sin⁻¹x/√(1 − x²) dx.
qa.e: t = sin⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/2: [t²/2] = π²/8.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx.
qa.e: t = x², dt = 2x dx: (1/2)∫₀¹ eᵗ dt = (e − 1)/2.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₁^e (log x)/x dx.
qa.e: t = log x, from 0 to 1: ∫₀¹ t dt = 1/2.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) cos x/(1 + sin x) dx.
qa.e: t = 1 + sin x, from 1 to 2: ∫dt/t = log 2.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin x) cos⁵x dx using t = sin x. The resulting t-integral is
qa.e: cos⁵x dx = cos⁴x · cos x dx = (1 − t²)² dt, and limits become 0 to 1.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): After substituting t = g(x) in ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx, we may evaluate the t-integral using the new limits g(a) and g(b), without returning to x.
Reason (R): As x runs from a to b, t = g(x) runs from g(a) to g(b), and f(g(x)) g′(x) dx becomes f(t) dt.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: R is exactly the substitution rule for definite integrals: the integrand turns into f(t) dt and the limits turn into g(a) and g(b). So A is true and R is its reason.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁² |x³ − x| dx.
qa.e: Sign of x³ − x: + on [−1, 0], − on [0, 1], + on [1, 2]. The pieces are 1/4, 1/4 and 9/4, total 11/4.

qa.q: If ∫₁⁴ f(x) dx = 6, what is ∫₄¹ f(x) dx?
qa.e: Reversing the limits changes the sign (P1).

qa.q: Evaluate ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of dx/(1 + √(tan x)).
qa.e: Using P3 and adding the two forms, 2I = π/3 − π/6 = π/6, so I = π/12.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₂⁸ |x − 5| dx.
qa.e: Split at 5: ∫₂⁵ (5 − x) dx = 9/2 and ∫₅⁸ (x − 5) dx = 9/2. Total 9.

qa.q: Applying P3 to ∫₀² x(2 − x) dx gives which integral?
qa.e: P3 replaces x by 0 + 2 − x = 2 − x, turning x(2 − x) into (2 − x)x, the same function.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): ∫ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0 for any integrable f.
Reason (R): ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = −∫ from b to a of f(x) dx.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Put b = a in R: I = −I, so I = 0. R gives A directly.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁¹ sin⁵x cos⁴x dx.
qa.e: f(−x) = (−sin x)⁵ cos⁴x = −f(x), so f is odd and the integral over [−1, 1] is 0.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₋₂² x² dx.
qa.e: x² is even: 2∫₀² x² dx = 2 × 8/3 = 16/3.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x(1 − x)⁵ dx.
qa.e: By P4, it equals ∫₀¹ (1 − x)x⁵ dx = 1/6 − 1/7 = 1/42.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴x/(sin⁴x + cos⁴x) dx.
qa.e: Adding I with its P4 version gives 2I = π/2, so I = π/4, whatever the power.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(2π) cos⁵x dx.
qa.e: cos(2π − x) = cos x gives 2∫₀^π cos⁵x dx, and cos(π − x) = −cos x makes ∫₀^π cos⁵x dx = 0.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) log sin x dx.
qa.e: Adding I with ∫ log cos x and using sin x cos x = (sin 2x)/2 gives 2I = I − (π/2) log 2, so I = −(π/2) log 2.

qa.q: Evaluate ∫₀^π x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx.
qa.e: P4 gives I = π∫₀^π sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx − I, so 2I = π[−tan⁻¹(cos x)]₀^π = π(π/2), and I = π²/4.

qa.q:

Reason (R): sin⁷x is an odd function.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: sin⁷(−x) = −sin⁷x, so by P6 the integral over a symmetric interval is 0.

qa.q: Find the area bounded by y = x³, the x-axis and the lines x = 1 and x = 2 (square units).
qa.e: Area = ∫₁² x³ dx = [x⁴/4]₁² = 4 − 1/4 = 15/4.

qa.q: Find the area under y = 2x + 1 from x = 0 to x = 2 (square units).
qa.e: ∫₀² (2x + 1) dx = [x² + x]₀² = 6. As a trapezium: (1/2)(1 + 5)(2) = 6.

qa.q: Find the area bounded by x = y², the y-axis and the lines y = 1 and y = 3 (square units).
qa.e: Using horizontal strips, area = ∫₁³ y² dy = [y³/3]₁³ = 9 − 1/3 = 26/3.

qa.q: For the area between a curve x = g(y), the y-axis and y = c to y = d, which integral is used?
qa.a: ∫ from c to d of x dy
qa.e: Horizontal strips have length x and width dy.

qa.q: Find the area bounded by y = sin x and the x-axis between x = 0 and x = 2π.
qa.e: ∫₀^π sin x = 2 and |∫ from π to 2π of sin x| = 2. Total area = 4.

qa.q: Find the area bounded by y = x³, the x-axis and the lines x = −2 and x = 1.
qa.e: |∫₋₂⁰ x³ dx| = 4 and ∫₀¹ x³ dx = 1/4, total 17/4.

qa.q: Find the area between y = 3x + 2, the x-axis and the lines x = −1 and x = 1.
qa.e: The line crosses at x = −2/3. Below: 1/6. Above: 25/6. Total 26/6 = 13/3.

qa.q: Find the area under y = |x + 3| from x = −6 to x = 0.
qa.e: Two triangles each with base 3 and height 3: 9/2 + 9/2 = 9.

qa.q: Find the area bounded by y = x² − 1 and the x-axis between x = −1 and x = 1.
qa.e: The curve is below the axis there: ∫₋₁¹ (x² − 1) dx = 2/3 − 2 = −4/3, so the area is 4/3.

qa.q: Find the area bounded by y = cos x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = π.
qa.e: 1 from [0, π/2] plus |−1| from [π/2, π] = 2.

qa.q: Why can ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx be smaller than the area between the curve and the x-axis?
qa.a: Parts below the axis give negative contributions that cancel positive parts
qa.e: Integrals are signed; area counts every part as positive.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The area bounded by y = x, the x-axis, x = −2 and x = 2 is 4 square units.
Reason (R): ∫₋₂² x dx = 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Area = 2 + 2 = 4 (two triangles). R is true too, but it is the signed integral, which is exactly why it cannot explain the area.

qa.q: Find the area enclosed by the circle x² + y² = 9.
qa.e: Area = πa² with a = 3, i.e. 9π.

qa.q: Find the area of the region in the first quadrant enclosed by x² + y² = 16 and the axes.
qa.e: One quarter of π(4²) = 16π/4 = 4π.
